Taiwanese officials raise alarm over interference by China in elections that will shape fortunes of ruling party

Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local elections that will shape the fortunes of the ruling Democratic Progressive party (DPP) as it navigates an increasingly precarious set of relationships on the global stage.

Saturday’s vote will choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across 22 districts. Unlike the presidential elections, in which foreign policy is often a key issue, the local elections, held every four years , are largely focused on bread-and-butter issues such as housing affordability and wealth distribution.

Nevertheless, China looms large over the vote, which takes place against the background of intense military pressure from Beijing . China claims Taiwan as part of its territory despite never having ruled the self-governing island. Taiwanese officials have raised the alarm over thousands of incidents of suspected misinformation or election interference, and certain candidates have been subjected to harassment from the Chinese authorities. There have also been reports of hundreds of China-linked AI-generated videos spreading disinformation about Taiwanese politicians disliked by Beijing.

Beijing calls the allegations of election interference “completely fabricated”. Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for China’s Taiwan affairs office, said the allegations “stir up anti-China sentiment to win votes”.

Wei-Ting Yen, a political scientist at Academia Sinica, Taiwan’s national research academy, said: “Even though local elections are not about China, the outcome of local elections will have huge implications for cross-strait relations.”

Most races are a tight competition between a candidate from the ruling DPP and the main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT). The KMT promotes closer ties with Beijing, and its chair, Cheng Li-wun, travelled to China this year to meet Xi Jinping, China’s leader. Xi has vowed to unify China with Taiwan, and has not ruled out using military action to achieve that aim.

Yen said if the KMT loses some of its traditional strongholds, Beijing “may need to reconsider what is the most effective strategy for influencing Taiwanese people”.

One of the most contentious votes is the race for Taipei mayor, an office that has been held by the KMT for three decades. The DPP has selected as its challenger Puma Shen, a national legislator whom Beijing declared a “diehard separatist” in 2024. It is the first time a candidate under sanctions by Beijing has run to be mayor of Taiwan’s capital city. In the neighbouring New Tapei City race, the DPP’s Su Chiao-hui is also proving to be a ferocious challenger to the incumbent KMT.

Shen said in a recent interview that even if he didn’t win, the capital’s mayoral race was “a slap to China” because it proved that “democracy works here in Taiwan”.

Huang Bo-kai, a 23-year-old law student, said his top concern was cross-strait relations and how US-China relations were evolving. “The world’s three major powers are increasingly willing to flex their muscles: the US attacking Iran, Russia attacking Ukraine. I think Taiwan could very well be the next target [of China],” he told the Guardian.

Taiwan’s president, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te, is detested by Beijing and has taken a bolshier stance on cross-strait relations than his predecessor, Tsai Ing-wen, who was admired for her ability to drum up support in Washington while walking a delicate tightrope to avoid angering China.

Lai has pushed for greater spending on weapons to deter military aggression from China. The government has proposed a record 18% increase in defence spending for next year, including for drones and missiles, taking it above 1tn Taiwan dollars (£23bn) for the first time.

But many Taiwanese voters would rather that money was spent on more immediate economic issues. Lev Nachman, a political scientist at National Taiwan University, said the national leaders of the DPP and KMT had been notably absent from the mayoral races, reflecting the extent to which campaigns were focused on local issues.

Going into the campaigns for the 2028 presidential elections, Lai would “try to take advantage of the momentum that [Shen] and Su have built for the DPP,” Nachman said, noting that support for those candidates would not necessarily translate into support for Lai.

Tony Yeh, a Taipei man in his 70s, said: “To put it simply, the authorities should do more to boost the economy and buy fewer weapons.”

Taiwan’s economy has boomed this year, largely thanks to the pivotal role that its semiconductor industry plays in the global artificial intelligence rally. The economy grew by more than 14% in the first nine months of the year, the fastest rate in 50 years. But nearly 70% of workers earned less than the average monthly wage of 49,152 Taiwan dollars (£1,137) in the same period.

Yeh said: “Most traditional industries are having a really tough time.”

William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “The issues that really are going to determine their votes are livelihood issues including the stagnant wage, the astronomically high housing price, the affordability issue, and how the government can better make sure Taiwan’s incredible economic boom fuelled by the global AI growth is going to be distributed more evenly.”

Other voters have more niche concerns. Walking her dog in a park, Kuo Wei-tong, a nail salon worker, said policies affecting pets were among her top concerns.

“People are having fewer children and getting more cats and dogs,” she said. “I think that’s something worth giving serious consideration to as well.”

stories.title: Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
stories.summary: Other countries have rerouted trade in response to his first tariff salvo, now they are looking beyond Trump's tenure.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 7 hours ago

There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.

Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.

"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.

Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.

The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.

Still, the US is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.

The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.

It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.

The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".

The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.

US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China Published 23 hours ago

New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause Published 12 hours ago

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow Published 6 days ago

However, the most interesting spot to focus on is closer to home for Trump. Over half of Canada tariffs are authorised under "Section 338" of the 1930s Smoot-Hawley act. There is already a Senate Bill to repeal them, and it is possible that there would be enough rebel Republicans in the House and Senate to threaten to over-ride any Presidential veto. The incoming Senate Finance Committee chair Ron Wyden last week said Democrats were focussed on "figuring out a way to beat Trump and his veto".

Before that an interim deal is being sought, and Democrat senators such as Chris Coons are appearing on Canadian TV, telling CBC , external : "Frankly, if you can get an interim deal, I'd take it, and then put it to us in the new majority to legislate an even better deal."

The rest of world is watching the machinations in Washington and also looking beyond Donald Trump's tenure.

It pays to look at how the initial Trump trade-quake has reshaped the pattern of world trade already.

The rest of the world has rerouted its trade flows around Donald Trump's tariff wall, proving far more resilient than expected. In cash terms, China's exports so far in 2026 are down about 8% on 2024, but that is more than 25 times made up for by its increased exports to everywhere else.

Canada has seen flat exports to the USA since tariffs, fewer cars and lumber, but pricier flows of energy. Its exports, especially commodities, to the rest of the world have rocketed.

This means that next month's G20 summit at the president's Miami resort is an important moment. In general US allies have not rocked the boat, accepting the lower level of tariffs as part of the new reality. Could the middle powers choose to upset their host in Florida next month?

The bigger question however, is how much the Democrats decide to keep of the America First trade agenda. It will not be all, but nor will it be nothing. Economists now expect some of these tariffs to stay in place for years.

stories.title: UK to pay 'participation' fee to deliver EU deals
stories.summary: Details of the contribution towards EU running costs have been revealed in new legal documents.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The UK has agreed the deals in a bit to cut red tape for British companies

Published 4 hours ago

The UK will pay a "participation fee" to the EU as part of the deals agreed by Andy Burnham, according to legal documents.

The surcharge will go towards the running costs of EU agencies and systems required to deliver two of the agreements unveiled by the prime minister last week.

It will be paid in addition to a contribution towards costs that broadly mirrors how EU members contribute to the bloc's shared budget, the documents show.

The government has sought to contrast the financial costs of the deals against their overall effect on the economy, which it estimates will receive an eventual boost by billions a year due to increased trade.

The government is yet to publish an estimate of overall additional costs, but officials said they expected them to be in the low tens of millions per year and "massively outweighed" by predicted economic gains.

British ministers had already said they were prepared to pay towards administrative costs required to implement deals to re-link the UK to the EU's carbon trading regime, and align Britain with the EU's food standards.

Now, details of how the payments will be calculated have been revealed in treaties to deliver the two agreements, which are meant to take effect during 2028.

Legal text for a third agreement agreed last week, on youth visas for 18 to 31 year olds, is expected to be published in the coming days.

Fee details

According to the treaties, the payments will be made as a share of the running costs of three EU agencies, as well as various systems that will be used to implement the food standards and emissions deals.

The bulk of the payments, to be made in euros, will come in the form of an "operational contribution" in proportion to the size of the British economy compared to that of the EU.

This broadly mirrors the way in which EU member states split the cost of their main contributions towards the bloc's overall budget.

But in addition, the UK will also pay a "participation fee" set at 4% of its main contribution figure.

The government has pointed to the 2021 Brexit trade agreement negotiated by the Conservatives, which also applied an additional surcharge to UK contributions towards the cost of relevant EU programmes.

However, any additional contributions are likely to be seized upon by opponents of the latest deals.

Ministers had declined to enter into specifics of the fees during negotiations on the treaties. On Sunday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the latest deals agreed by Burnham were "not about cost to the taxpayer".

'Extraordinary powers'

It comes as the government published separate legislation granting it broad powers to incorporate new EU laws required to implement the agreements, without having to hold a full vote each time.

The food standards deal in particular will mean Britain will have to align with scores of current EU food-related laws that have been updated since Brexit, along with future rules in these areas.

The government argues the new powers are required because it would be impractical to run a full parliamentary process each time UK legislation needs to be updated to make the agreement work.

But it has prompted criticism from opposition parties, because the UK no longer has voting rights at the EU to shape European legislation.

The government argues the UK will get a say on new rules, with the treaty texts confirming British experts can be consulted when new EU laws are being drawn up, with the UK granted "observer" status in certain meetings.

But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham was showing "disdain for the democratic process" by asking for a "blank cheque to install and enact EU law".

"The prime minister is telling MPs to hand him extraordinary powers whilst having no idea what the EU will actually agree to," she added.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has argued the Burnham's deals would take Britain back into "much of the European Union's single market".

He added: "European economies are not growing as fast as ours. The idea that getting closer to the EU will mean growth for us is a myth."

In a Thanksgiving post, the US president seeks investigation after blue wave of Democrats unseat Republicans

Donald Trump has alleged without evidence that economic figures published by the US federal government before this month’s midterm elections were “fake” and demanded an investigation after voters roundly rejected his Republican party.

In a holiday message on social media tinged with bitterness, the US president wished a happy thanksgiving “to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%”.

While revisions to official economic figures are commonplace, Trump has tried time and again to challenge trust in economic data that does not support his claims that a historic boom is underway in the US.

The US Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), an agency within the US Department of Commerce, calculates gross domestic product, or GDP, numbers.

“Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Thursday. “This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error”.

Trump has repeatedly claimed since taking office in January 2025 that an economic “golden age” is taking hold on his watch. Many Americans have been grappling with a higher cost of living, however – exacerbated by the economic fallout of his war on Iran – and backed Democrats in the midterms.

Trump continued his acerbic well-wishing for “a very Happy Thanksgiving to all of those people that have worked so hard to bring our Country to the Radical Far Left” as well as “those who want to redistribute Property, so that all of the hardworking people that have built up, over a lifetime, a certain Wealth, will now be forced to distribute it throughout the Country, even to those who refuse to work”.

And he revisited another ongoing beef with the news media over his controversial focus on White House renovations and decorations. “I want to commiserate with those reporters and citizens who don’t understand filth, dirt, lack of maintenance, and corruption, and are upset with me because I took time out of my very busy schedule to fix the 17 broken windows, numerous chipped and decaying columns, broken, dilapidated, and missing moldings, and lack of a proper plaster and paint job on the White House.”

The sarcastic intervention continued with a message of thanks to “the murderers, drug dealers, and criminals of all shapes, sizes, and colors” whom he claimed are “mostly gone now”.

“Happy Thanksgiving to them anyway, even though from faraway lands,” he concluded. “We miss you dearly, but you will never be back, and America will never allow what you have done to us to happen again!”

Democratic senator Chuck Schumer, vying to be majority leader in the chamber following his party’s victories in this month’s election took a more conventional approach , wishing “everyone in New York and across America a joyous and restful Thanksgiving holiday with your friends and family”.

Hakeem Jeffries, whom Democrats have nominated to be the first Black speaker in the House of Representatives, also played it straight. “Happy Thanksgiving to everyone in the community and throughout our great country! Grateful for the civil servants on the job who are working through the stormy weather to keep everyone safe,” he posted on X. “May God bless you all.”

stories.title: Burnham says UK net migration now under 'sufficient' control
stories.summary: It comes after annual net migration fell to 77,000 - the lowest level this century, excluding the coronavirus pandemic.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 26 November 2026

Andy Burnham said he believes there is now a "sufficient degree of control" of net migration in the UK after it fell to 77,000 in the year to the end of June.

The prime minister said the country is "getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see" but added that there was more work to do.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said it is the lowest recorded net migration estimate since 1997, excluding the coronavirus pandemic.

The Conservatives said the fall was "mainly a result of changes" they made in government, while Reform UK said the figures were "no cause for celebration".

UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall Published 12 hours ago

Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats Published 14 hours ago

What are the planned changes to immigration rules? Published 3 November

Net migration is a measure of how many extra people are added to the population in a given year.

An estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated, according to the ONS.

In the previous 12 months, UK net migration was recorded as 204,000. It peaked at 944,000 in the year to March 2023.

The 77,000 net migration figure released on Thursday comes more than 16 years after former Conservative leader David Cameron pledged to cut it to below 100,000 before he came to power in 2010.

Speaking to broadcasters, Burnham said: "These figures begin to answer what the public has been saying, we want to see much greater control over the system.

"I'm not going to say all of the work is done and I don't want to appear complacent, but I think we're finally, as a country, getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see."

It was put to Burnham that some people may argue this was a "benefit of Brexit", in light of his desire to explore closer ties with the European Union .

Asked if freedom of movement should be up for discussion as part of the UK's future relationship with the EU, Burnham said in his reply: "I don't think you can say that Brexit did anything other than weaken control of immigration in this country."

The ONS said net migration had "fallen to levels not typically seen since the 1990s".

The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.

A fall had been expected because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp argued the Conservatives should receive credit for the decrease in net migration.

He added: "We now need to go even further with an annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels.

"British and European people are leaving in their droves because of Labour's high taxes whilst non-EU immigration remains far too high."

Liberal Democrat asylum and immigration spokesman Paul Kohler said Britain faces "serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services".

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage welcomed the drop in numbers, but said he was concerned about "a lot of high skilled big tax paying people" leaving the UK and being replaced by people "who are paying far less in tax".

Meanwhile, his party's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick said the fall "came about solely because I went to see Rishi Sunak" in 2023 whilst an immigration minister in the Conservative former prime minister's government.

Jenrick, who defected to Reform earlier this year, told the BBC: "I threatened to resign unless he made a series of changes. He did".

"And as a result of those changes to the immigration system, we've got where we are today".

But he added that the changes "didn't go as far as I wanted to," adding this had been behind his resignation from the Tory government a few days later.

A Green Party spokesperson said: "Creating a harsh environment for migrants and asylum seekers is not a measure of success."

stories.title: Burnham joined by former PMs at Widdecombe service
stories.summary: Hundreds of guests attended including Andy Burnham, David Cameron, Liz Truss and Boris Johnson.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham and a number of previous prime ministers attended the service

Published 26 November 2026

Andy Burnham was joined by former prime ministers as he attended a memorial service for the late politician Ann Widdecombe.

Hundreds gathered for the Service of Remembrance at Westminster Cathedral on Thursday afternoon, including David Cameron, Liz Truss, Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage and deputy leader Richard Tice, along with former Conservative Chancellor Philip Hammond and Speaker of the House of Commons Sir Lindsay Hoyle, were also in attendance.

Bishop James Curry, the Auxiliary Bishop of Westminster, led the service after the Archbishop of Westminster, Richard Moth, was taken to hospital earlier.

Reform UK's chairman Lee Anderson, deputy leader Richard Tice and leader Nigel Farage were among those at the service

Moth, who is the head of the Catholic Church in England and Wales, underwent tests after he "felt unwell", Westminster Diocese said.

During the memorial, tributes were paid by Widdecombe's nephew, Reverend Roger Widdecombe, and independent crossbencher Lord Alton of Liverpool.

Widdecombe's nephew said his aunt's death was "a tragedy," but added the service was to "pay tribute to Aunt Ann" and "celebrate and thank God for a life well lived".

He said: "Words such as integrity, brave, kind, delightful, indefatigable, interested, tireless, fun, all express something of the amazing woman that Ann was."

He noted his aunt was "certainly a lot of fun," recalling family anecdotes which prompted guests to laugh.

Finishing the eulogy, he said: "We loved her very much, and we'll miss her."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham shakes hands with former prime minister Rishi Sunak at the service

The service, which lasted about 70 minutes, featured a motet, a psalm and two hymns sung by the Westminster Cathedral choir.

The prime minister was later seen leaving the cathedral with former prime ministers Rishi Sunak and Boris Johnson.

Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK's justice spokeswoman, was found dead at her home in Haytor, on Dartmoor, Devon, on 9 July, aged 78.

Politicians past and present gathered for the service remembering Ann Widdecombe

Joshua Kerry, 28, of Byrley Road, Rotherham, South Yorkshire, was charged with her murder.

A trial before a High Court judge is scheduled for 8 June, and a plea and case management hearing on 29 January.

Widdecombe's family announced plans for a public memorial service following her death.

The late politician served as Conservative MP for Maidstone and the Weald in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

Away from politics, she appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing in 2010 and was a runner-up on Celebrity Big Brother eight years later.

In the 1990s she converted to Catholicism, a move she later described as the best decision she ever made.

stories.body:
Beijing says new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’, while Brazil ‘will not yield to this type of threat’

Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU

Beijing has said it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash.

Among the suggested levies on 14 major trading partners announced on Wednesday, China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. It would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.

“China urges the United States to correct its erroneous practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” the Chinese commerce ministry spokesman, He Yadong, said at a regular briefing. “China will closely monitor developments and reserves the right to take necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.”

Brazil was also singled out in the announcement after trade talks stalled.

Brazil’s government said on Wednesday that “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat”, adding in its statement that the “unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process”.

It voiced particular indignation at US proposals for higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products”.

The Trump administration said that the new tariffs would be consistent with trade deals that the US reached last year with dozens of countries. They are being imposed under a law that allowed the president to target countries the US had found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base”.

The Trump administration’s new tariff rates would be capped at lower ​levels ‌agreed under ​trade deals ​that have already been concluded or remain under negotiation.

The administration will seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing on 25 January, suggesting the final duties won’t take effect until February or March.

Trump met his counterpart, Xi Jinping, in Shenzhen last week but the escalation in tariffs will not be a surprise to China, Dan Wang, a director on Eurasia Group’s China team, told AFP news agency.

The US and China last year reached a trade truce but that is set to expire on 10 January 2027. Trump and Xi are expected to meet again in Miami on the sidelines of the G20 in December.

“It has become a pattern before every major top leader summit,” Wang said, adding that she did not think the new measures would derail relations between Washington and Beijing.

“Xi has a high incentive to keep bilateral relations stable leading up to the 21st (Communist) party congress in October 2027,”Wang said.

A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China was ‌a source of ⁠excess capacity.

“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements secured between Trump andd Xi .

Earlier, China’s foreign ministry restated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” said the spokesperson Guo Jiakun.

Greer told CNBC that the administration was proposing a “broad exemption” for $30bn worth of Chinese goods in line with the deal. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this – they know what we’re proposing,” Greer said. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”

Some US analysts criticised the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.

China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined”, said Derek Scissors, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.”

after newsletter promotion

The EU said it rejected the premise of new tariffs and expected the US to stick by a deal struck last year. “The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” said the European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill.

Vietnam’s trade ministry said it was ⁠working with the US to complete its trade deal as soon ⁠as possible and would coordinate with relevant US agencies.

It added it was “preparing ​and submitting ​rebuttal comments on the ​preliminary findings as well as on inaccurate submissions ​and allegations ‌made by ​interested ​parties”.

In response to the US announcement, the Indian government denied it had any structural excess capacity in ⁠any sector, ⁠adding that it remained committed to an early conclusion of ⁠a trade deal between the two countries. Greer has said the tariff ⁠on Indian imports would be capped at 17% if a trade deal was struck.

Taiwan was also earmarked for new tariffs but Taipei on Thursday said it was confident it would keep its existing ⁠15% tariff rate.

Taipei and Washington signed trade deals in January and February of ‌this year, which secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other tech products that account for ​more than 70% of Taiwan’s exports to the US.

Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the EU, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland and Thailand.

Tokyo’s top government spokesperson, Minoru Kihara, said it was “regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced”.

Singapore’s government said it was “very disappointed” with the proposals and denied it was protecting its domestic market or subsidising manufacturing.

Trump’s latest round of tariffs may be here to stay despite the Democrats’ electoral sweep in the US midterms. Some Democrats will probably support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.

However, the Democratic senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the finance committee next year, said he would “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos”.

He added: “This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.”

Bank of England warns of increases for millions coming off fixed deals over next three years as interest rates rise

Business live – latest updates

More than 400,000 UK homeowners will face a £500-a-month increase in their mortgage payments over the next three years, as rising interest rates heap extra pressure on households, the Bank of England has said.

The Bank’s financial policy committee said on Thursday that out of the 7 million borrowers coming off fixed-rate deals before December 2029, about 6.5 million would have to cough up extra funds to cover their home loan payments.

For about 3.4 million borrowers the monthly increase would be less than £100, while for a further 2.7 million it would be £100-£500. The increase would be even greater for those borrowers coming off much lower interest rates, with about 430,000 likely to see their monthly mortgage payments surge by more than £500.

Warnings about the increases came after policymakers at the Bank of England hiked interest rates from 3.75% to 4% this month. The Bank also hinted at another increase in interest rates to combat inflationary pressure caused by the Iran war. The financial markets have predicted three quarter-point rate rises by summer 2027.

Over the next year, about 1 million households will see their payments rise by almost £200 a month.

The news will put further pressure on Andy Burnham’s efforts to offset cost of living pressures, with the chancellor, John Healey, having used his first budget to promise “breathing space” for hard-pressed consumers .

The figures came a day after the energy regulator for Great Britain raised the cap on household energy bills by 26% .

The Bank’s deputy governor for financial stability, Sarah Breeden, said it was important to keep in mind that households would “face this [mortgage] shock with strong balance sheets”.

She said household debt was relatively low, at a level last seen in the early 2000s. “So they start from a position of some resilience. And secondly … while there’s a distributional effect and some households would be hit more than others, in aggregate we think this is absorbable.”

The Bank also raised concerns on Thursday about cybersecurity and AI threats after recent outages at Google and Microsoft laid bare businesses’ growing dependence on outside technology, and how “disruption at a single provider” could “affect many firms at once”.

The Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, told a press conference that policymakers were worried about “open weight” AI – open source models, many of which are being developed in China. “These models can be run more cheaply … Safeguards may be disabled or removed more easily. This could make more advanced AI capabilities more readily available and useful to malicious actors,” he said.

The Bank also raised fears for the first time about emerging quantum computing capabilities potentially undermining the encryption technology that protects essential financial transactions.

Bailey said quantum computing would have been at the top of everyone’s mind this year, but that the surprise development of frontier AI models had overshadowed those concerns.

after newsletter promotion

“It’s slightly moved quantum into the background … as you can see, we are very intentionally saying we can’t forget about quantum computing, it’s still coming down the track,” he said.

He emphasised that it was crucial, and possible, for banks to start to build up their defences against quantum risks, even while the technology was in nascent development. “It could have powers that go beyond what we’re seeing with frontier AI and have substantial power to undermine cryptography,” he said.

The Bank said the evolving risks reinforced the need for “significant and sustained investment by the financial sector in building resilience”, adding that banks needed to have credible arrangements to ensure they could bounce back quickly from any disruption and maintain “vital financial services”.

The financial policy committee acknowledged this would place competing demands on lenders’ tech experts and management teams, but added that a failure to take action would “compromise firms’ operational resilience with potential system-wide implications”.

The Bank also announced plans on Thursday to further reduce capital requirements for UK banks, as part of a wider package that it said could unleash an extra £175bn in lending capacity. However, extra funding could end up being used to pay out shareholders and investors.

Watch: What we know about Trump's Thanksgiving tariffs

Published 25 November 2026

The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.

The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions, including Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.

The White House began investigating the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal .

China is facing the highest tariff rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35%, with others facing either 20% or 25%.

The US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the proposed tariffs together with extensive reports of how each jurisdiction's trade practices purportedly impact American commerce.

The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year and have to go through rounds of public consultation and, potentially, hearings.

Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of a good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing products.

Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.

The proposed tariffs will affect goods from China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.

The USTR's Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy".

Jamieson Greer, US trade representative

He said that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression".

They also employ "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America's manufacturing base", Greer said.

But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade.

Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs.

Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy.

Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them.

Trump's so-called Liberation Day tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year

These new levies are build on a "stronger legal foundation" under US law compared with Trump's April 2025 Liberation Day tariffs, Singapore Management University economics lecturer Chang Pao-Li said.

Trump previously invoked emergency presidential powers to impose tariffs that have since been struck down, while his latest approach relies on the USTR's authority to impose tariffs to address certain foreign trade practices, she said.

The levies are still likely to face legal challenges, but there has been a "historical precedent" for such tariffs remaining in force, Chang said.

Many tariffs imposed under Section 301 - a law that allows the US to probe and retaliate against foreign trade practices - during Trump's first term remained in effect during his successor Joe Biden's administration.

However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer.

"The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note.

The additional tariff burden is likely to be small because a limited number of goods are subject to the new duties, Brown added.

Jurisdictions affected by the new wave of tariffs have voiced their disapproval over the Trump administration's move.

Washington has also proposed a 10% tariff on goods from Brazil, as part of a separate investigation over what it says are "harmful trade practices" undercutting American workers.

Brazilian authorities expressed their "outrage" at the announcement, saying that the move is aimed at pressuring the government to change regulations around issues like digital trade.

The South American nation faces duties on finished aircraft and sugar sold to the US.

"Brazil will not yield to such threats," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's office said.

The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed.

The latest tariff rate is "not consistent" with the reality of bilateral economic-trade cooperation between the US and Vietnam, Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister Bui Thanh Son said.

The Japanese government said the US tariffs were "regrettable", while the Singapore government said it disagrees with the White House's findings and that it is engaging the USTR to explore ways to reduce the tariff.

South Korea's trade minister said the proposed 15% tariff will be "more than a decent outcome" as it would fall in line with a previously agreed limit with Washington.

Last year, Seoul pledged $350bn (£267bn) in US investments in exchange for lower tariffs as part of a trade deal.

Trump tariffs on Asia: Which economies were hit hardest? Published 1 August 2025

China's growth accelerates as AI boom helps boost exports Published 19 October

US trading partners have been "waiting for this shoe to drop" and have argued that they are being wrongly accused of producing too much, said the Asia Society Policy Institute's Wendy Cutler, a former senior US trade negotiator.

"Many believe that China, not them, should be the target for US action," she added.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun described the new tariffs as a form of "political manipulation", describing as "false" the US claim that China produces more than it can consume.

The tariff announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and the AI race.

The two countries have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold.

Despite last week's meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, the two sides made no announcement on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January.

Beijing has remained vague on how it will respond but for now seems "prepared to live with the new rates provided they don't exceed 20%", Cutler said.

stories.body:
Personal independence payments (Pip) are UK-wide benefits that are meant to help people with long-term health issues cope with the extra costs associated with their conditions. But it’s controversial – from the application process to who qualifies.

Sir Stephen Timms, the disability minister, has published a long-awaited report into Pip, recommending a raft of changes to the system.

Here’s what experts made of his findings.

‘Constant dread’ during the application process

Stephanie Allan, Research Associate in Mental Health & Wellbeing, University of Glasgow

Humanising the benefits system, as Timms claims his review will, is crucial. As part of our research , participants told us that applying and being assessed for disability benefits such as Pip has caused psychological distress, particularly for those applying due to conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder or schizophrenia.

We’ve been told assessments can feel like “being on trial”, with constant dread of unexpected letters coming through the door, and can even cause re-traumatisation.

The review’s call to reduce unnecessary reviews and improve communication between assessors and applicants may address these issues – as may its suggestion of training assessors in trauma-informed practice. This means they should offer consistency and transparency in explaining how decisions are made and not minimising people’s difficulties.

Some people living with serious mental health problems face profound challenges and struggle to do things many people take for granted. The report proposes fast-tracked paths for peopel who have “serious, well-evidenced conditions whose impact on their daily life is clear”. But it’s ambiguous which conditions this will cover, and this could also cause worry for potential Pip recipients.

While the Timms review acknowledges the impact of stigma, our work emphasises how negative media reporting and politicians’ speeches about disability benefits can cause distress, especially if it frames claimants as burdens. It can also influence how people respond, and make them even more afraid to participate in society.

People with fluctuating mental health problems have told us that fears of being falsely reported for fraud by neighbours and community members can make them avoid activities such as volunteering, exercise , or even taking part in clinical research that could improve mental health for them or others in future.

Training on trauma-informed care is arguably not enough on its own. Without stronger legal safeguards – such as independent oversight when things go wrong – the power imbalance between claimants and those in charge remains intact.

Furthermore, reforming the claiming process by itself will not make people feel safe if political rhetoric and media narratives continue to frame disabled people as a burden.

Every day is different when you’re disabled

Steve Atkin-Teillet, Lecturer in Law, Nottingham Law School

The nature of some conditions means that symptoms can fluctuate from day to day. The review found that in order to capture the varying nature of a claimant’s needs, the Pip application form should be changed so that it’s simpler for claimants to report what they experience.

This should be underpinned by better training for Pip assessors on the rules surrounding variances and fluctuations in what someone is able to do. This should not only include a requirement to assess whether someone can perform an activity, but also whether they can do so reliably.

Right now, a claimant should only be considered capable of a task if they can do it safely, repeatedly and in a reasonable amount of time. In 2024, I recommended that the new Pip form include these three elements under each activity the claimant describes, as well as on the government’s Pip advice page.

At present, people claiming Pip can be assessed by any type of medical professional. Someone applying for mental health reasons could be given a physiotherapist as their assessor. This is a concern, as claimants sometimes feel their assessor was not competent or well placed to understand their condition.

The Timms review proposes a specific Pip assessor role – but this doesn’t fully address concerns over competency. As it stands, it’s unclear how someone in this new role would be trained to assess a full range of potential disabilities and conditions.

More understanding of neurodiversity since Pip launched

Mindy Ptolomey, Lecturer in Disability Studies, University of Leeds

The review has highlighted that when Pip was designed and implemented – back in 2012 under David Cameron’s coalition government – it did not consider the barriers neurodivergent people face in everyday life. Neither did it take into account their needs in terms of the application process. As pointed out in the interim report of the review, long paper forms with no online version, rigid deadlines, and having to use the phone can all create barriers for neurodivergent people.

Read more: The Milburn report sets out a plan to improve the lives of young people who are Neet – experts respond

The review’s recognition of neurodivergent people’s needs is especially important as the diagnosis of ADHD and autism has increased in recent years. In the UK, new adult autism diagnoses increased more than tenfold from 2010 to 2023, and monthly referrals for ADHD diagnosis more than tripled between 2019 and 2024.

A government review published last month highlights that there is no evidence of widespread over-diagnosis. These increases are instead due to a range of factors like historical under-recognition and greater awareness.

It’s encouraging to see a continued commitment to involving disabled people during the design and implementation stages of any reforms. Disabled people were part of the review’s steering group and their views were included in a range of ways. However, more can be done to make sure the people who face the greatest barriers are included in shaping reforms. Involving neurodivergent people is important for ensuring the core purposes of Pip are delivered supporting disabled people’s independence, participation and autonomy.

Pip can make an important contribution to meeting the additional costs of being disabled, for those in and out of work. The review recommends linking the amount people will receive through Pip more closely to the additional costs they face due to disability or health conditions.

However, questions remain about how these costs will be identified and calculated. Previous data shows that it is difficult for disabled people to understand the additional costs of being disabled, especially when you’ve had a condition all your life, which is the case for neurodivergent people.

Mental health conditions could face cuts

Sarah Ledden, Research Associate in Population Mental Health, King’s College London

One key element of the proposed reforms is to only provide Pip to those who incur additional costs due to a long-term health condition or disability. The challenge here will be creating appropriate mechanisms to assess these costs, without repeating current difficulties the system has in evaluating fluctuating and ‘harder-to-see’ conditions.

The Department for Work and Pensions recently released a research report which aimed to understand the disability-related needs that create additional living costs among Pip recipients. It indicated that people with mental health conditions were less likely to have additional costs for equipment and travel needs, though they did more often have paid treatment needs (such as counselling).

However, these people experience employment and income gaps, earning 32% less than people with no such conditions, and higher levels of financial hardship . This indicates that there are often financial challenges for people with mental health conditions, but many of these costs may be hidden or cumulative.

If the transition to a new benefit is managed poorly, with proposed impact assessments not designed to capture these types of costs, it risks people with mental health conditions being left behind. The Timms review has recommendations around understanding inequalities in experiences and outcomes of different groups, which will be vital in ensuring the system works.

The DWP’s evidence published with the review reported that only 1 in 5 Pip claimants reported having a single condition. Most people reported multiple conditions. Only 4.4% of total Pip claims are those solely claiming for depression and anxiety, with these more often reported alongside other conditions.

The rise in these cases is based on the “primary condition” reported on Pip claims, although this is in line with evidence that these conditions are rising in the general population.

Previous research from our team on Pip receipt among people who accessed specialist mental healthcare found that receiving Pip is related to greater clinical need (including diagnosis type and longer time receiving care). If the government aims to reduce welfare spending by assessing mental health Pip claims using stricter criteria, this may not have as big an impact as they expect.

stories.body:
Germany’s far right is on the rise, with current polls suggesting the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has the backing of 28% of voters nationally. This makes it the most popular party in the country, ahead of German chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats at 20%.

However, there are geographical divides in the AfD’s support. Polling indicates that over 35% of voters in east Germany support the AfD compared with 20% in the west. My research offers insights into why, 36 years after Germany was reunified, there are differences in voting behaviour between both sides of the country.

In 2019, two video artists, advised by me and other researchers and historians, interviewed 26 people about their lives in a divided and reunified Germany. These people were all born in 1975 and grew up in different areas of the country: east or west Berlin, Baden-Württemberg in the south-west or Brandenburg in the north-east.

My analysis of the interviews found that west Germans consistently stated their lives had not changed as a result of reunification. Torsten*, an interviewee from Baden-Württemberg, said: “For me, everything was fine before and everything is still fine.”

On the other hand, all of the east German interviewees experienced the transition from the planned-economy socialism of the German Democratic Republic to the social market economy of the Federal Republic of Germany as a profound change.

As 14-year-olds at the time of reunification, their entire lives were turned upside down. Nathalie, who grew up in east Berlin, where she still lives, said: “That’s when the chaos began, I’d say. My nice, orderly world just wasn’t so orderly anymore. I felt like I’d lost my footing.”

Reunification did present opportunities for east Germans, including greater freedom in choosing a career and new chances to travel. When asked what changes the fall of the Berlin Wall had brought about, Matthias from Brandenburg explained: “For me, that was the biggest opportunity of my life. I don’t know where I’d be now if that turning point hadn’t happened the way it did.”

But people like Matthias also had to witness businesses from former East Germany struggle to withstand new economic competition. The closure of unprofitable firms and the massive job cuts in companies that were sold, primarily to west German investors, meant they saw their parents and grandparents lose their jobs and towns and neighbourhoods left desolate.

Some of the interviewees spoke of a feeling of “devaluation” and of being treated as second-class citizens. Matthias recalled travelling to West Germany on a student exchange programme and hearing the parents of host students ask whether teenagers from the east knew how to eat with a knife and fork.

The majority of the west German interviewees knew little about the German Democratic Republic era and the challenges associated with the fall of the Berlin Wall. And many were unaware that inequalities between the two sides of the country persist.

These include the fact that less wealth is passed down through the generations in eastern Germany and that a higher share of households in western Germany own their homes than in the east. West Germans also occupy a large share of top positions in east German companies.

As a result, the west German interviewees did not understand the dissatisfaction felt by many in the east. Elke, from Baden-Württemberg, said in reference to east German complaints: “Man, you’ve been here for so long now. Why are you complaining? You’ve built such a great life for yourself here, and you’ve been given so many opportunities.”

For east Germans, on the other hand, the effects of inequality are part of everyday life. The people interviewed as part of the project had come to terms with the fact they are not listened to and that no understanding is shown towards them.

Bridging the divide

This feeling of not being heard or understood could be a leading factor in why many people in eastern Germany are voting for the AfD . The party is promising radical change and, in eastern regions, promotes nostalgia for the German Democratic Republic era.

According to a national survey released after the Saxony-Anhalt regional election in September, where the AfD secured victory with 43.8% of the vote, many east Germans see economic disparities and a lack of recognition for their achievements as an obstacle to national unity.

That is why it is important for east and west Germans to talk to one another, helping them come to terms with the past and shape the present together. This is the aim of outreach projects I run with my colleagues.

In one of these projects, Connecting Generations , we present video installations based in part on a selection of our interviews with the Germans born in 1975. We display the video installations in public spaces such as museums, memorial sites, libraries and adult education centres throughout Germany.

The aim is to provide Germans with spaces for encounter and dialogue. West Germans learn about the history of division and the period of change, and can familiarise themselves with the perspectives of people from the east.

Another project, Generations in Dialogue , focused on schools. We presented a video installation partly based on the same interviews and invited eyewitnesses into school classes to talk about their experiences.

After all, greater knowledge and understanding of all perspectives are needed to bridge the political divide between east and west Germany.

stories.title: FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns
stories.summary: The post FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Rx Roulette

A ProPublica investigation last year found the Food and Drug Administration failed to regularly test generic medications that doctors warned about or drugs coming from factories with serious quality and safety violations.

The Food and Drug Administration will test more prescription drugs for impurities and other dangerous quality lapses under an expanded program described by safety experts as a critical step to better protecting America’s drug supply.

About 90% of prescriptions in the United States are for generic drugs, many manufactured thousands of miles away in countries that include India and China. Until now, the FDA has only periodically tested a sampling of those drugs to see if they were safe or worked as effectively as the brand-name medications they are meant to replicate.

Read More

Last week, the FDA announced it will test more often and identify poorly performing drugs for further study.

The agency said it will buy the medications from retail pharmacies and wholesale distributors, but it did not say how many drugs it plans to test or how frequently. A spokesperson did not answer questions about how the FDA would select drugs for testing or how it would hold manufacturers accountable for inferior products, beyond posting the results on its website. Still, drug-safety experts said the expansion helps address long-standing concerns that some suppliers sacrifice quality to keep costs low — and that the FDA has for years looked the other way.

“All drugs, regardless of where they are manufactured, must meet the same FDA standards for safety, effectiveness and quality,” the FDA spokesperson told ProPublica.

A ProPublica investigation last year found the agency routinely relied on the drug companies themselves to do their own testing even as doctors, researchers and the Department of Defense warned that essential medications were contaminated or ineffective. On its website, the FDA said it has relied on a “more targeted, risk-based” approach to testing since 2018, choosing samples of drugs that have safety, effectiveness or quality concerns. The agency publicly reports the results on its website and notes that a majority of the tested drugs meet its standards.

ProPublica, however, found the agency for years failed to regularly test both the generics that have worried outside experts and drugs coming from factories that amassed so many serious quality and safety violations they were ultimately banned from the U.S. market. ProPublica later used FDA data to create Rx Inspector , a first-of-its-kind tool that allows consumers and doctors to look up the inspection records of the factories where more than 40,000 generic drugs are made.

Researchers have repeatedly urged the FDA to test more often. In fiscal year 2025, the FDA reported testing 46 different drugs, and for 29 of those drugs, the agency only tested one manufacturer . All but one passed every test.

The FDA’s new testing regime is “a huge validation of the research that we’ve been doing raising concerns about the quality of generic drugs,” Dr. Kevin Schulman, a professor of medicine and health policy at Stanford University, said of the FDA’s new testing program. “This is a great effort on their part.”

In February, senators also introduced a bill targeting transparency in the drug supply chain process, in part because of similar public concerns.

In response to questions about how it would decide which drugs to sample and how results would drive future enforcement, the FDA spokesperson said the initiative will “help the FDA identify potential drug quality issues faster and will provide more information the agency can use to decide if further action is needed.”

Experts say they ultimately hope the FDA’s program will work alongside independent testers to shift the generic drug market to be competitive on quality rather than price. While the agency can focus on weeding out the worst actors, independent labs can test manufacturers against one another to find the most effective products, said retired Col. Vic Suarez, a former medical supply-chain commander. A similar system is already used at the Department of Defense.

“It’s an important thing because they will probably catch extreme violators of regulatory standards, so that’s a good thing,” Suarez said. “But you also need to have a complementary system where you’re actually raising the bar.”

ProPublica previously engaged an independent lab, Valisure, to test several generic versions of three of the most prescribed drugs in the United States and in two cases identified irregularities that experts said could compromise their effectiveness.

“I think, high level, the idea that we should be doing more testing is fantastic,” said David Light, the co-founder of Valisure. “I think there’s so much growing energy behind that.”

stories.title: Democrats Vow to Shield Smithsonian From Any Trump Overhaul
stories.summary: The post Democrats Vow to Shield Smithsonian From Any Trump Overhaul appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A top House Democrat with oversight of the Smithsonian Institution affirmed the agency’s independence and told ProPublica she’ll investigate any political pressure coming from the White House.

A top congressional Democrat announced she will investigate the Trump White House’s potential overhaul of the leadership and curatorial decisions at the Smithsonian Institution, the independent agency that oversees 21 national museums.

In a letter sent on Tuesday to the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents, Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine, cited ProPublica’s recent story on the draft plans by a White House staffer targeting one of the Smithsonian’s most prominent museums, calling the reporting “extremely concerning.”

Read More

Pingree, who is slated to lead the subcommittee that controls the Smithsonian’s funding in the next Congress, said the plans revealed in the ProPublica story align with the administration’s broader efforts to interfere with the Smithsonian, which receives federal funding but is governed by a 17-person Board of Regents whose members include the chief justice of the United States, members of Congress, the vice president and private citizens.

In an interview with ProPublica, Pingree said that she intended her letter to put the Smithsonian governing board on notice that the incoming Democratic majority in Congress is monitoring the institution to make sure the board upholds its responsibility to keep the agency independent from political pressure.

“No White House employee riding on the Metro gets to design a plan for what future exhibits look like or gets to veto staffers or exhibits at the Smithsonian,” Pingree said. “That’s not how it works.”

Pingree told ProPublica that she plans to use her powers as chair in the next Congress to aggressively look into what she called the Trump administration’s meddling with the Smithsonian and to expose those efforts to the broader American public.

“We fully intend to dig deeper than has been done in the past,” she said.

Pingree’s letter comes in response to ProPublica reporting on a 25-item list of possible changes that, taken together, would amount to an unprecedented attempt by the White House to control the content and personnel of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, which attracts nearly 2 million people a year.

Those reforms include firing many of the museum’s top officials; rolling out a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance”; introducing new K-12 learning materials such as a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage”; and unveiling a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.

The draft plans were visible on the laptop and in handwritten notes of a White House staffer who was riding a D.C.-area Metro train in late October. A nearby commuter took pictures of the materials and sent them to ProPublica reporters, who in turn verified the information. It’s unclear what kind of reception the plans have received inside the Trump White House. The staffer and White House did not respond to requests for comment for the story.

Also on Tuesday, Lonnie Bunch, the Smithsonian Institution’s outgoing leader, responded to ProPublica’s reporting in a message sent to employees. “The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote in his letter . “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.”

Pingree was not the only member of Congress who responded to ProPublica’s reporting with a pledge to defend the Smithsonian’s independence.

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., said on social media that if he becomes chair of the Senate Rules Committee — which has jurisdiction over the Smithsonian — in the next Congress, “we will protect it from Trump’s interference and overreach.”

“The Smithsonian is NOT a federal agency, it is an independent, nonpartisan organization overseen by Congress – not the White House,” Padilla wrote .

Incoming Congressman Fred Wellman, a Democrat elected this month to represent the suburbs of St. Louis, responded even more forcefully to ProPublica’s reporting on social media.

“Over my dead body,” he wrote .
