stories.title: Inside the Trump Administration’s War on the International Criminal Court
stories.summary: Marco Rubio publicly advocates a return to might-makes-right barbarism by threatening to use military force against the ICC. The post Inside the Trump Administration’s War on the International Criminal Court appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Marco Rubio (Shutterstock)

Originally published in TomDispatch .

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has once again attacked the global system of laws, norms, and principles instituted to place limits on international armed violence. Advocating for a return to might-makes-right barbarism during a keynote speech on Friday, Rubio threatened to use military force against the International Criminal Court, which prosecutes individuals accused of the gravest atrocities. Warning that if the ICC was “foolish enough to try to enforce their paper decrees on Americans, our answer will probably be the same as the Roman general Pompey when he said to those who were trying to invoke their city’s charters against his legions. … ‘Stop quoting laws to men with swords.’”

Rubio’s effort to undermine the principles and rules that regulate the means and methods of warfare and the humanitarian protection of civilian populations, sick and wounded combatants, and prisoners of war is part of the Trump administration’s wide-ranging effort to upend the rules-based international order that the U.S. has championed — but often failed to abide by — since World War II.

Speaking before the conservative Federalist Society at the National Lawyers Convention in Washington, D.C., Rubio disparaged the ICC as a “fake court” and “an unelected world tribunal, which claims to supersede the laws and constitutions of sovereign states, even those who never signed up for it.”

Rubio’s tirade was the latest salvo in a long-running campaign against the ICC by President Donald Trump’s administration, which has vowed to cripple the court. In October, after former ICC judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, Trump — who has relentlessly campaigned for the award — was enraged and derided the South African jurist as “a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of.”

Hours after the award was announced, the U.S. imposed sanctions on the ICC. These latest sanctions are intended to turn the judicial organ into an economic pariah. They prohibited the court from conducting dollar-denominated transactions, froze its U.S.-based assets, and barred the judicial body from using the U.S. banking system or working with American institutions — effectively blacklisting the court.

The ICC was created by the international community to investigate and prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide, and the crime of aggression — when one country uses armed force against another without legal justification. The Hague, Netherlands-based court is unique as a permanent judicial organ capable of prosecuting anyone, infantry soldiers and sitting heads of state alike, for humanity’s gravest crimes if they are committed in the territories of its 125 member states. The ICC is critically a court of last resort that will only intervene when domestic jurisdictions either fail to hold their own service members and political leaders accountable, or when state parties to the court call for an investigation.

While the Trump administration’s timing in sanctioning the ICC was notable, this latest strike against the court is just one facet of the Trump administration’s yearslong campaign to — in the words of Rubio’s State Department — “ dismantle ” it. The effort dates back to 2020, when the first Trump administration imposed sanctions on ICC officials after the court opened an investigation into alleged U.S. war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Afghanistan .

Overturned by the Biden administration in 2021, the first round of U.S. sanctions against the court were replaced last February by a new series targeting the court’s chief prosecutor, its two deputy prosecutors, and six of its judges. All of these judges had either investigated the actions of U.S. nationals in Afghanistan or were part of the ICC’s decision to issue arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for their co-perpetration of “the war crime of starvation” and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

Though the litany of prior U.S. sanctions against the court impacted the lives of those nine individuals and their families — cutting them off from their bank accounts, emails, and blocking their travel — the actions were piecemeal and did not fully upend the work of the court.

Now, all of the ICC’s U.S.-based partner organizations have six months to completely cut ties with the court or face legal retribution. What’s more, since the current global economic system is built upon the U.S. dollar, international — particularly European — organizations often preemptively abide by U.S. sanctions even if their workings fall completely outside of America’s jurisdiction. For example, when the French company Axa terminated its life and health insurance contracts with the ICC on October 1, the insurer reportedly cited the escalating campaign by the U.S. against the court.

Absent the implementation of effective countermeasures — like amending and enforcing the EU Blocking Statute , which can shield EU individuals and businesses from “unlawful” third-country sanctions — this latest move by the U.S. may not kill the ICC, but it will cut off the judicial organ’s blood supply.

Victors’ Justice?

For over 80 years, the U.S. has enjoyed the privilege of proscribing — and not necessarily abiding by — international law. American representatives served as the chief arbiters of the post-World War II Nuremberg and Tokyo military tribunals that prosecuted Nazi and Japanese war criminals, which are seen by many in the field as the birthplaces of modern international criminal law. American arbiters, notably U.S. Supreme Court Justice Robert H. Jackson, led the victors of the Second World War as they tried and prosecuted their former adversaries for novel notions of wrongdoing, including crimes against peace and crimes against humanity. These newly defined criminal acts form the bedrock of the ICC’s jurisdiction.

At the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, all 25 major Japanese leaders were convicted, with seven receiving death sentences. Judge Radhabinod Pal of India argued for the acquittal of all 25. In his dissent , he complained that the tribunal dispensed victors’ justice. He said that America’s atomic strikes on Hiroshima and Nagasaki were among the most criminal acts of the conflict, yet immune from prosecution.

Indeed, the international criminal justice system was never intended to hold the U.S. or its allies accountable. And in the decades since, consecutive U.S. administrations have wielded the nation’s political and military strength to avoid any semblance of international legal oversight.

Although relations with the court have oscillated over the course of Democratic and Republican administrations, the U.S. has always been wary of the court’s potential jurisdiction over American nationals. From the court’s conception, in which the U.S. played a role, the global hegemon has continuously shown its disdain for the court’s territorial jurisdiction. While the ICC cannot prosecute any American nationals for their actions in the U.S., it does have jurisdiction over acts undertaken, by U.S. nationals or otherwise, within the territories of its member nations including Afghanistan, Libya, and Palestine.

Under the Clinton administration in the 1990s, the U.S. was one of only seven drafting nations to initially veto the Rome Statute — the international treaty that created the ICC — due to its concerns over the court’s territorial jurisdiction. Later, in 2002, the same year the ICC was established, the George W. Bush administration signed the Hague Invasion Act into law. The act, which is still in effect, grants the president the legal backing to use military force against the court in order to free any U.S. or allied person held or imprisoned by the ICC. The Bush administration subsequently pressured dozens of countries to agree to never transfer U.S. nationals to the ICC, and threatened to cut military assistance, cease counterterrorism operations, or cut humanitarian aid if these states did not comply. Though relations with the ICC thawed somewhat under the Obama administration in the 2010s, the U.S. has never shown a substantial interest in joining the court and has worked for years to restrict its jurisdiction.

Soon after taking office, Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ordered a mass purge of senior judge advocates general. Among their many functions, JAGs historically educated military leaders on the laws that prohibit the use of the U.S. military in domestic law enforcement and ensured commanders were aptly informed of the international legal obligations to protect civilians and prisoners of war. When asked about the mass layoffs in February 2025, Hegseth explained that the action was taken to remove potential “roadblocks to orders that are given by a commander in chief.”

In a concerted effort to further “ maximum lethality ,” Trump and Hegseth additionally gutted the Pentagon’s Civilian Protection Center of Excellence and the broader Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response program in the early months of 2025. The budding program, which the majority of U.S combatant commanders urged Hegseth to maintain, was established in 2022 to prevent, reduce, and respond to civilian casualty incidents. Stark cuts to the program’s manpower and funding coincided with a rise in civilian casualties reported in U.S. military operations in Iran , Yemen , Somalia, and in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea .

When taken together, the administration’s cuts to internal legal mechanisms and policy programs intended to maintain law and protect civilians, as well as its ongoing attempts to dismantle the ICC, can be seen as two aspects of a larger campaign to eradicate all avenues of military oversight.

The Fight for Justice Will Continue

The sweeping courtwide sanctions against the ICC are formidable for the same reasons they are survivable: They aim to isolate the court from its broad system of support. The international criminal justice system depends on evidence. This evidence is not found in The Hague; it is brought to it by an array of local, national, and international investigators, researchers, watchdogs, and atrocity survivors.

The evidence needed to confirm the genocide in Palestine; the U.S. bombing of the elementary school in Minab, Iran; and the extrajudicial killings of fisherman in the Caribbean would not exist without the networks of dedicated researchers, local journalists, and courageous survivors. And the work of these people, while critical to the court’s functions, will continue, even if the court is dismantled brick by brick.

The ICC has strongly condemned the U.S. sanctions. ICC President Tomoko Akane has said that the court will “continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes.” Pillay has also used the publicity stemming from her Nobel Peace Prize to showcase the court’s work. She further dedicated her award to “all the survivors of international crimes” as well as the international jurists “whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign.”

In his speech on Friday, Rubio took aim at those very jurists, declaring that the U.S. would never submit to the “sterile vision of radical judges or soulless global bureaucrats.” He claimed that this “global elite” was using international law as “an instrument to advance their interests under the pretense of universal principles.” This was, in fact, a stark about-face for Rubio, who was an advocate for international law during his 14 years as a U.S. senator. He even co-sponsored a resolution encouraging other nations to support the ICC’s investigations of Russian war crimes in Ukraine.

Rubio claimed that those who advocate for the restraint of law over all nations are anti-American. “For these people — the fundamental purpose of the law, American law and international law alike, is to weaken the United States,” he claimed. “It is to hinder the American government’s ability to defend American interests at home and abroad.” He continued, “There is nothing — there is nothing — in our history or the history of any other great nation that requires us to recognize the authority or legitimacy of any of these ridiculous ideas.”

Prior to Rubio’s speech, however, Pillay offered up a differing vision of America. In her estimation , Americans are not the singularly self-interested, lawless, reprobates envisioned by Rubio but a people who eschew limitless violence and value humanitarian principles. “I know,” she said, “that Americans support the principle of ending impunity for these serious crimes and that they support justice and accountability.”

stories.title: Why Accountability Cannot Depend on Political Power
stories.summary: The International Criminal Court has ruled that Myanmar has committed genocide. The United States has sanctioned the ICC. Which approach will prevail? The post Why Accountability Cannot Depend on Political Power appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Students participate in class in a shelter in the camp on October 28, 2019 in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh. 27 year old Rohingya refugee Shamima Bibi is currently running 16 schools for women in different tents around the camps. (Allison Joyce/Getty Images)

This month, two international courts have faced tests that expose a central weakness in the international legal order. In October, the United States imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court as an institution , extending earlier measures against its judges and prosecutors. On November 19, the International Court of Justice delivered its judgment in the genocide case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar, finding that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya.

Together, these developments raise an uncomfortable question: does accountability under international law depend on the political power of the state concerned?

In law, the answer should be no. The international legal system rests on the principle of sovereign equality between states , enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations . All states are bound by the same rules and obligations, whatever their size or their political, economic, or military weight. In practice, however, whether a violation is followed by consequences depends not only on its gravity but also on the balance of power, and on whether influential states are willing to cooperate with international institutions.

The weakness lies less in the absence of legal rules than in the limits of enforcement. Judgments of the International Court of Justice are binding on the parties, but the Court has no independent enforcement arm. Article 94 of the UN Charter allows a party to refer non-compliance to the Security Council, which may make recommendations or decide on measures to give effect to the judgment. That route is vulnerable to politics: the permanent members retain the power of veto . The best-known illustration is Nicaragua v. United States. After the ICJ ruled against Washington in 1986, the United States vetoed a Security Council draft resolution calling for compliance . A mechanism designed to support the Court’s rulings can therefore be blocked by the very state against which the judgment was delivered.

The Gambia v. Myanmar demonstrates another side of the problem. In 2019, The Gambia, a small West African state, brought proceedings alleging that Myanmar had violated the Genocide Convention in its treatment of the Rohingya. The Court indicated provisional measures in 2020 and upheld its jurisdiction in 2022. On November 19, 2026, it delivered its judgment on the merits and found that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya during the 2017 clearance operations in northern Rakhine State. The Court also found violations of Myanmar’s obligations to prevent and punish genocide and to enact the necessary legislation to give effect to the Convention.

This is a landmark legal finding. But a judgment, however significant, is not the same as accountability. Its practical effect will depend on whether Myanmar complies and whether other states are prepared to support implementation.

The International Criminal Court, which prosecutes individuals rather than states, faces pressure of a different kind. The October measures followed earlier U.S. sanctions on its judges and prosecutors . The Court has strongly rejected the institutional sanctions, describing them as an attempt to obstruct its work. Its ability to continue operating matters, but resilience should not obscure the principle at stake. The independence of an international court depends not only on legal texts but also on the political environment in which it operates. It should not hinge on the goodwill of the most powerful states, particularly when the Court’s work touches their interests.

Sanctions are another tool used in the name of accountability, and research on their effectiveness is more nuanced than the headlines suggest. A 2024 review by Daniel Drezner finds that economic coercion can be more effective than scholars once believed, while also highlighting substantial unintended consequences. Sanctions can impose heavy costs without changing a state’s behaviour, and ordinary people often bear much of the burden. Their effects vary with the objective, design, and degree of international cooperation behind them. Imposing costs is not the same as securing accountability. The contradiction is especially stark when a tool intended to enforce international norms is directed at the institution charged with applying them.

These problems do not harm only the states directly concerned; they weaken the international system as a whole. When the prospect of accountability varies with a country’s influence, confidence in the impartiality of international institutions erodes. International law becomes less able to regulate relations between states and more likely to be seen as an instrument shaped by political alliances and strategic interests.

The result is not simply selective enforcement. It is a loss of confidence in the idea that international obligations apply equally.

States can help address this problem without creating entirely new institutions. Those that support the ICC can take practical steps to protect its independence and ensure that sanctions do not obstruct its mandate or the work of those cooperating with it. Members of the Security Council can also consider commitments not to use the veto to block action in response to non-compliance with ICJ judgments. Such measures would not eliminate political influence, but they could make it harder for power to determine whether international law has consequences.

The judgment in The Gambia v. Myanmar demonstrates that international courts can make consequential findings, including against states accused of grave violations. But its significance will be measured not only by what the Court has declared but by what happens next. International law cannot guarantee that every judgment will be enforced immediately. It must, however, insist that accountability does not become a privilege reserved for states with less political power. A legal system in which the likelihood of enforcement varies with the strength of the state concerned risks losing one of its most important foundations: the confidence that it is a common framework governing all states rather than a tool whose effectiveness depends on the balance of power.

stories.title: War Reveals a Global Food System Tethered to Fossil Fuels
stories.summary: The Iran war has shuttered refineries in the Persian Gulf and throttled the production of sulfur, which is critical for making fertilizer needed to feed the world. The crisis, expected to raise grocery prices, hints at an unintended consequence of the fossil fuel phaseout. Read more on E360 →

stories.body:
A pile of sulfur at an oil refinery in Cartagena, Spain. Sulfur, a byproduct of refining, is needed to make phosphate fertilizer. Angel Garcia / Bloomberg via Getty Images

ANALYSIS

The Iran war has shuttered refineries in the Persian Gulf and throttled the production of sulfur, which is critical for making fertilizer needed to feed the world. The crisis, expected to raise grocery prices, hints at an unintended consequence of the fossil fuel phaseout.

By Fred Pearce • November 24, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Millions of farmers around the world are living in fear that their crop yields will falter in the coming months. They blame the Iran war, which has reduced supplies of the phosphate fertilizer vital for a successful harvest by 40 percent and raised its price beyond the reach of many.

But few farmers will likely know that their reliance on Persian Gulf states for much of their phosphate fertilizer is an outgrowth of a global effort more than 30 years ago to banish a major environmental scourge — the sulfur emissions from power plants that caused acid rain.

Those efforts required oil and natural gas refineries in the Gulf and elsewhere to strip sulfur from their products. That waste sulfur swiftly became the go-to feedstock for making sulfuric acid, the world’s most widely used industrial chemical, and one that is essential when processing phosphate rock to make phosphate fertilizer. Sulfur prices tumbled and, unable to compete, almost all the world’s sulfur mines shut. Soon, nearly half of internationally traded sulfur was being supplied by refineries in the Gulf. Or it was until those supplies were cut off in 2026.

Today, more than 95 percent of the world’s sulfur comes from oil and natural gas refineries.

There isn’t yet any reliable data on crop yields following the fertilizer drought: Most crops are still in the ground. But farmers from Brazil to India to southern Africa await with trepidation the impact on their upcoming harvests.

The rest of the world should be equally concerned. Analysts expect the crisis will cut crop yields in 2027 and beyond, raising food prices everywhere for years to come. The World Food Programme warns that, in combination with El Niño , the shortage could bring hunger to at least an additional 49 million people.

Meanwhile, analysts warn that the potential impact of the sulfur crisis on fertilizer production is likely to be just a foretaste of what will happen as the world phases out fossil fuels. An end to refining oil and natural gas would also halt the supply of waste sulfur at a time when demand is set to increase due to greater need for fertilizer and for refining metal ores for the fast-growing batteries market, says Mark Maslin, a geographer at University College London who has tracked the trade.

“My concern is that green tech outbids the fertilizer industry for the limited, more expensive sulfur supply,” he says, “creating an issue with food production, particularly in developing countries.”

A farmer spreads fertilizer on his land in Indian Kashmir. Firdous Nazir / NurPhoto via AP

Using waste sulfur from refineries to make sulfuric acid should be a textbook example of how circular economies work, with one industry’s discards becoming the feedstock for another. Tens of millions of tons of waste sulfur from refineries is used in the manufacture of everything from rubber tires to paper. Before the war, the fertilizer industry absorbed more than half of the world’s available sulfuric acid to extract phosphorus from rocks and make a product that helps to feed the world. Sulfuric acid is also used to extract copper, nickel, and cobalt from ores to make the batteries that run electric vehicles — a critical part of international efforts to reach net-zero carbon emissions by midcentury.

And yet that green virtue in 2026 turned into a liability. During the Iran conflict, damaged production plants and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the main shipping route from Gulf refineries to sulfur markets, cut off 45 percent of the world’s trade in this strategically vital waste product. (While Gulf producers have been able to export some oil and natural gas through pipelines to the Red Sea, there are no pipelines that can handle dry, solid sulfur.)

This sudden sulfur shortfall has caught governments and producers without a Plan B, says MacDonald Amoah, an analyst of critical minerals for the Payne Institute for Public Policy at the Colorado School of Mines. Because sulfur has been regarded as a waste product, it has been little monitored by trade bodies. As it happens, this industrial material, essential for feeding the world, has no strategic reserves.

Many fertilizer producers have shut down because their ultimate customers, farmers, can no longer pay for the product.

In the 1980s, acid rain was a headline-grabbing environmental scourge. Emissions of sulfur dioxide from power stations burning sulfur-rich fossil fuels turned the rain across Europe and much of North America as acidic as lemon juice. Forests from the Appalachian Mountains to the Carpathians in Eastern Europe lost foliage and died; acid-drenched soils released toxic metals, killing fish in rivers and lakes.

The scourge was high politics, too. Canada’s environment minister complained to a visiting Ronald Reagan that his nation’s damaged forests and lakes were at the end of a “gigantic exhaust pipe” that began in the eastern United States. Swedish and Norwegian governments blamed British power stations for their hundreds of fishless lakes.

Governments eventually acted, requiring the scrubbing of sulfur dioxide from power station flue gases. Power companies in turn demanded that refiners supplying oil and natural gas remove the sulfur at source. The result of this international clean-up was a vast new waste stream of elemental sulfur that soon found a market as a feedstock for manufacturing sulfuric acid.

By century’s end, the world was awash with cheap waste sulfur. The market price had fallen by 80 percent, forcing mines from Sicily and Mexico to the salt domes of Texas out of business. Today, more than 95 percent of the world’s sulfur comes from oil and natural gas refineries, and almost half of international trade is through the Strait of Hormuz.

Cargo ships anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Bandar Abbas, Iran. Amirhosein Khorgooi / AP Photo

Most discussion about the resource implications of the Iran war has concentrated on disruption to the Gulf’s oil and natural gas exports. But the war has also hindered the production of the two most critical fertilizers in the world: nitrogen-based ammonia, which is made in the Gulf using hydrogen extracted from natural gas, and phosphate fertilizer, whose manufacture requires sulfur extracted from hydrocarbon refining. The conflict has cut the amount of nitrogen supplied to farmers by about a quarter but phosphate supplies by 40 percent.

As the war has progressed, the supply of sulfur has continued to shrink. In May, China, the world’s largest exporter of sulfuric acid, banned sales to foreign manufacturers to protect its own fertilizer supplies. Then in August, Ukrainian drones struck Gazprom’s Astrakhan gas processing plant, knocking out 60 percent of Russia’s sulfur production.

With supplies cut and prices up by more than a third, sometimes exceeding $1,000 per metric ton, much of the sulfur that has been available has been snapped up by the mining industry, which can afford the higher prices. The price hike has left phosphate fertilizer producers in a bind. Many have shut down because their ultimate customers, farmers, cannot pay for the product. Mosaic, one of the world’s biggest manufacturers, more than halved its U.S. production in 2026 and has announced plans to shut one plant for six months starting in December. “Without affordable sulfur,” production superintendent Hector Mier said last month, the company was “forced to curtail production. That means less fertilizer for farmers and less food grown in American farmland.” Saudi and Brazilian plants have also closed.

As less fertilizer is added to soils, says an analyst, there will be an “erosion of agricultural productivity in many countries.”

Brendan Rice, an agribusiness analyst for the Washington, D.C.-based International Food Policy Research Institute, warns that as less phosphate fertilizer is added to soils, there will be “a slow-rolling erosion of agricultural productivity in many countries” stretching through 2027 and beyond.

The first clear signs of the downturn may emerge in the next three months with the harvest of rice in India and Thailand, soy in Brazil, and corn in southern Africa. Amoah says it will “lock in grocery inflation for years.”

What will happen if the Gulf conflict continues to restrict sulfur supplies?

There is no immediate prospect of a revival of sulfur mining. Only two mines remain open: the Osiek Mine in southern Poland and the Kawah Ijen volcano on the Indonesian island of Java, where a few hundred intrepid miners armed with hand tools clamber down into the crater to dig out yellow blocks of elemental sulfur, which they haul to the surface in bamboo baskets. Neither mine could quickly increase production, analysts say. And a widespread reopening of closed mines would be a costly and risky enterprise when Gulf production of cheap sulfur could resume at least as quickly.

A miner gathers sulfur from Kawah Ijen, an active volcano on the Indonesian island of Java. Oscar Espinosa / SOPA Images / LightRocket via Getty Images

There is sulfur stockpiled at a few refineries — notably some 10 million metric tons around tar-sands deposits in the Canadian province of Alberta, some of which is sent to fertilizer manufacturers in Canada and the U.S. But scaling up distribution quickly for the international market would be challenging. “Every tonne must be excavated off the block, trucked to a melting site, melted, formed, and railed to Vancouver for vessel loading,” says Fiona Boyd , a director of London-based Acuity Commodities. “[It’s] a lengthy and expensive process.”

Experts predict that Gulf supplies of sulfur will eventually resume. But that will only postpone the day, says Maslin, when the world faces a long-term sulfur crunch as demand rises while supplies falter.

On the demand side, most observers expect a rapid increase in the use of sulfuric acid as more metals are refined to make batteries. And as the world’s population continues to rise, feeding more people will also likely require more sulfur to make more phosphorus fertilizer. Overall, Maslin sees the market growing by around 60 percent to 400 million metric tons by midcentury.

Farmers could reduce their use of synthetic fertilizers by nourishing their soils with animal manure and farm waste.

But at the same time, he says, supply is set to crash as the world’s energy system decarbonizes, with consumption peaking and then falling sharply over the next three decades, slashing the production of sulfur waste at refineries. In 2022, Maslin and his University College London colleagues calculated that shifting away from fossil fuels “could create a shortfall of sulfuric acid as large as 320 million [metric tons], or 130 percent of present-day production.”

The supply crunch would drive up the cost of sulfur, Maslin said. Then, as now, farmers — and the world’s food supply — would be the likely losers.

To address the shortfall, farmers could reduce their dependence on both nitrogen and phosphate fertilizers by nourishing their soils organically. Animal manure and organic farm wastes are rich in both chemicals. But few agriculturalists expect such methods to do more than moderate rising demand for synthetic fertilizer — and the sulfur needed to make it.

So where will the sulfur come from? We could go back to large-scale mining. Unlike some strategic materials, the world is not short of geological sulfur. It is the 13th most abundant element in the Earth’s crust, found in volcanoes, salt domes, and in sedimentary deposits created by the evaporation of seawater.

A tractor spreads fertilizer on a soybean field in Goias, Brazil. Mateus Bonomi / Anadolu Agency via Getty Images

But Maslin warns of the risks. “Direct mining of elemental sulfur is dirty, toxic, [and] destructive.” To minimize the damage, he says, “the world needs to cut demand by recycling and using alternative industrial technologies that avoid intensive use of sulfuric acid.” Widespread commercial recycling of sulfur has potential. Sulfuric acid is a major component of widely used lead-acid batteries, for instance. In the U.S. it is widely recycled along with lead.

Another approach is to cut demand for sulfur’s biggest use — making phosphate fertilizer — by recycling the phosphates found in human sewage, which is where much of the material used to grow our food ends up.

More than half the world’s population is now connected to sewage systems. Sewage sludge from treatment works may contain industrial contaminants but is generally considered safe for application to cropland and often sold or given to farmers in developed countries, notably the U.K. and the U.S. Sludge incinerators in Japan and Germany sell their leftover ash, still rich in phosphates, either to farmers or to fertilizer manufacturers. Willem Schipper, a Dutch consultant in industrial chemistry, calculates that current sewage systems worldwide could deliver around a million metric tons of phosphates each year. That is roughly 3 percent of what is mined each year, but it would trim the need for both sulfur and phosphate, a rock that is itself in increasingly short supply.

By removing phosphates from raw sewage at treatment works, recycling would also reduce the environmental impacts of high levels of phosphates in rivers, where the chemical spurs the growth of plants and algae that block sunlight from penetrating the water and lower oxygen levels. So, while one version of a circular economy might falter as fossil fuels are sidelined, another, smaller circular economy could emerge.

stories.title: The Shenzhen Summit Supplants Yalta
stories.summary: The post The Shenzhen Summit Supplants Yalta appeared first on NOEMA .

stories.body:
A world made safe for spheres of influence.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

Pundits who dismissed the Shenzhen summit as a mere photo-op lacking substance missed the point. The significance of the conclave was precisely its enframing symbolism, showcasing a new world in which the rules-based order has been supplanted by spheres of influence accommodating each other.

The city of Shenzhen itself is a prism through which we can observe today’s power relations and the evolution of events over recent decades bringing us to this point.

Unplugged Computers in China’s Future Tech Hub

I first visited Shenzhen in 1986, arriving there by tram from Hong Kong and walking across the mainland border. There was barely any bustle, no crowds or traffic and a couple of tall buildings at the most. At our modest hotel, a squatting gardener was clipping the grass with a pair of scissors. The place still exuded the languorous vibe of the fishing village of 30,000 it had been not long before it was designated a “special economic zone” by Deng Xiaoping to attract foreign capital and technology.

On an inspection tour of sprouting industrial parks with then-former California governor Jerry Brown, our hosts proudly showed us what they called a tech hub. What then passed for “data centers” were cavernous, virtually empty warehouses with scores of desktop computers on worktables gathering dust — none were even plugged in.

What seemed embarrassing at the time turned out to be beyond impressive 40 years later. Shenzhen today is a literally glittering technopolis of 20 million people regarded as China’s “Silicon Valley” where Huawei, Tencent, DJI and BYD are all located. It is the center of gravity of China’s AI battle with the United States.

The invitation to visit had come some years earlier from Xi Zhongxun, then Party chief of Guangdong province (where Shenzhen is located) and the father of China’s current leader, Xi Jinping. The elder Xi had come to California in 1980 looking for investment in the special economic zone as a key platform of Deng’s policy of “reform and opening up” to the world. On that visit, he met Gov. Jerry Brown and toured the state, including stops at tech sites in the then-fledgling Silicon Valley (Apple and Intel were about it in those days) and Disneyland, where he gamely shook hands with Mickey Mouse.

Years later in 2012, when Brown was governor again for a second time, Xi Jinping, then-vice-president of China on his way to the top, visited California. The irony was not lost on either leader when the governor inquired whether China was interested in helping finance California’s bullet train, already in the works for nearly 20 years.

A Chinese delegation later met with the governor at the Peninsula Hotel in Beverly Hills to discuss possibilities, but the idea never panned out. Those who had once come cup in hand to the Golden State now offered financing terms too tough to abide. By 2026, China had built a 30,000-mile network of bullet trains spanning its vast country. California and the U.S. still have yet to build one.

On that 1986 trip to China, Brown and I also met at Zhongnanhai, the secluded leader’s compound in Beijing, with the ideology chief and youngest member of the ruling Communist Party Politburo at the time, Hu Qili. In a wide-ranging conversation that touched on topics from the “spiritual pollution” of Western influence to Tibetan Buddhism, Hu noted that the Chinese military had reduced its forces by one million soldiers. Many military installations, he said, were converting to commercial applications in light industry and heavy-truck production. Several military aircraft plants were now making refrigerators and motorcycles.

To this, Brown quipped, “If the army is making refrigerators, you must think the polar bear [what the Chinese called Russia] is hibernating.” Laughing, Hu simply replied that since Russia “couldn’t even consolidate control of Cambodia, it is only inviting great trouble to try anything with China.”

Opening then to America while hostile to an ebbing Soviet empire, Hu insisted that “China’s armed forces are sufficient to resist hegemonist efforts from the bear if they come.”

By the time I saw Hu again in 1988, Mikhail Gorbachev had come to power in the Kremlin, attracting some sympathy among reformers in China and inspiring a growing youth movement with his ideas of perestroika and glasnost. Enough of a thaw was in the works that Hu asked me to convey “fraternal greetings” to Aleksandr Yakovlev, then the Soviet party’s main reformist thinker, on my next stop in Moscow. Read Noema in print.

“The one key power left out of the 1945 Yalta talks that shaped the international order in the dying days of World War II is now setting the agenda for what comes next.”

The Tiananmen Turn

It was in that atmosphere that Gorbachev visited Beijing in May 1989 and met with Premier Zhao Ziyang as tensions with the authorities were mounting on Tiananmen Square. In the wake of the student massacre that June, the liberal-leaning Zhao was purged for revealing “state secrets” to Gorbachev by telling him that Deng, who would order the repression, remained the power behind the throne even though he had formally retired. Hu was also purged.

This was a “ludicrous accusation,” Gorbachev told me later. The real issue, as he saw it, was his advice that the student occupation should be defused politically through negotiation, not force. “I was confident a political solution could be found. I was wrong, unfortunately,” the last Soviet leader lamented.

Deng had drawn the line on Party control that Gorbachev was erasing in Moscow. Deng’s open palm on the economy clenched into an iron fist on political reform. Ever since, Gorbachev’s “new thinking” has been vilified in Beijing as a recipe for the collapse of the Party-state, and something to be avoided at all costs.

A World Safe For Spheres Of Influence

When Vladimir Putin emerged in the tumultuous years after the Soviet collapse, China’s sympathy with a more amenable Russia returned. As the post-Cold War years wore on, the “hegemonist threat” for China shifted to America, even as it prospered from the relationship.

In the end, China’s leaders came to strategically favor a trusted autocrat ruthlessly obsessed with dominating his own neighborhood over a meddling America endlessly endeavoring, in their minds, to subvert China’s governing system and keep the nation down. Party ideologues, Xi above all, are convinced that the American political class, implicitly if not explicitly, concurs with Bill Clinton’s remark when he was president that China was on “the wrong side of history.” Like many others in those days, Clinton wrongly presumed trade winds would blow open the society.

With a militarily mighty but economically feeble and dependent Russia at its side, China’s leaders have grown more confident in their capacity to contain America in a world made safe for spheres of influence.

The few words spoken for public consumption at the Shenzhen summit about zones of “civilizational values” and the primacy of state sovereignty over international law were code for the long-standing views of Xi and Putin, which the American president has now openly embraced.

Tech Trips The Thucydides Trap

At the first meeting of the Berggruen Institute’s 21st Century Council with Xi Jinping in 2013, the Party leader boasted that “we have never been closer to realizing the dream of Chinese rejuvenation” after the long climb back from colonial humiliation — invoking that history as if it were yesterday.

As Xi sees it, far from being on the wrong side of history, only the firm hand of the Communist Party could have brought the Middle Kingdom to where it is today and can take it where it must go tomorrow.

In 2015, then Premier Li Keqiang launched a “Made in China 2025” campaign with the goal of conquering the latest technologies from electric vehicles and batteries to artificial intelligence within a decade. Xi sees this conquest as rocket fuel for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, which he is determined to ensure does not fall behind the West and invite domination by outside forces, as it did during the Ming and Qing dynasties of the late 19th Century.

Strategists in Washington across the partisan landscape see China’s unrelenting resolve to reach its goals as an existential threat to America’s technological supremacy, and all that implies in terms of military might and geopolitical sway.

At our 2013 meeting, Xi pointedly raised an historical reference to “the Thucydides Trap,” whereby a rising power inevitably runs into conflict with an established power, only to say China would seek to avoid it. By now, though, it is clear that of all the contested issues between the U.S. and China, technology is most likely to trip the trap. The Nvidia episode is but one skirmish in a larger battle.

Shenzhen Supplants Yalta

If I were to have a conversation with the ideology chief on the Politburo today, as I had with Hu decades ago, here is what I would imagine him saying: “We have demonstrated we can go head-to-head with America on AI and technology. Today our military is reinvigorated. We have the largest navy in the world and are scaling up our nuclear arsenal toward parity with the U.S. and Russia. To be sure, America remains a formidable foe with the legacy of hegemonist ambitions. But let’s be serious. It is crumbling within. Its aging systems are plagued by outages. It can’t even build one bullet train.”

For Xi, hosting both leaders of the other great powers in Shenzhen, where China’s tech prowess is on full display, is the ultimate icing on the cake of rejuvenation. The one key power left out of the 1945 Yalta talks that shaped the international order in the dying days of World War II is now setting the agenda for what comes next.

stories.title: What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry
stories.summary: The post What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry appeared first on NOEMA .

stories.body:
Regulation alone won’t fix the conditions that have earned China the reputation of the “Wild East.”

Jane Qiu is an independent science writer in Beijing.

BEIJING — In March 2023, four-year-old Mei in Shanghai was diagnosed with a rare genetic mutation linked to developmental delay and autism-like traits. Although her condition was mild and she improved with therapy and special education, her parents remained worried about her future. Hopeful for a cure, they paid Qiu Zilong, a renowned neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and his team $860,000 to develop a customized gene therapy. The treatment, which used adeno-associated viruses to deliver gene editors to the brain, had been approved by Xinhua Hospital, a leading hospital for rare diseases.

On March 24, 2025, trillions of viral particles carrying gene editors were injected into Mei’s spinal cord. She soon developed a fever and kidney failure and died within days. A year later, Qiu’s team published its preclinical findings in Nature, which Chinese media hailed as “a world-class breakthrough.” Mei’s death and her family’s financial support were not mentioned.

Deaths in clinical trials are not unusual. What is shocking are the regulatory lapses revealed by an investigation published this July in Science and subsequently corroborated by a separate investigation conducted by the Shanghai municipal government, which released its findings last week. The treatment’s consent form, for instance, didn’t warn of the possibility of death. The hospital had approved treatment before toxicology findings showing liver and kidney damage in monkeys that received similar treatments. And, among other crucial omissions, the researchers failed to disclose Mei’s death.

Apparently, this was not an isolated incident. Several researchers told me that Chinese hospitals commonly fail to disclose adverse events. On Aug. 5, STAT reported another death in a gene-editing trial led by Shanghai-based HuidaGene, an incident that had remained undisclosed for about 15 months. (The Chinese team published their findings , including the fatal case, in Cell on Oct. 26.) A founder of a rare-disease organization in China told me, on condition of anonymity for fear of political repercussions, that she had encountered other trials for genetic disorders in which deaths had gone unreported. Recent revelations of undisclosed deaths in clinical trials conducted in China have prompted warnings against the use of Chinese data in U.S. drug development.

As someone who has reported on China’s ethical governance for two decades, this all feels like déjà vu. Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies — that have earned the country a reputation as biotechnology’s “Wild East.”

Back in 2006, patients flocked to China to receive unproven stem-cell therapies . When immunotherapies came into vogue a decade later, bogus advertisements for unproven interventions proliferated online until the health ministry stepped in after the high-profile death of 21-year-old student Wei Zexi. Two years later, biophysicist He Jiankui shocked the world by announcing the birth of the first genetically modified babies created using CRISPR technology.

The response in China to Mei’s death has been divided. Some netizens portray Qiu as a reckless scientist willing to gamble with patients’ lives. Others, including longtime acquaintances, describe him as a diligent scientist committed to helping patients. In some respects, Qiu represents the antithesis of He. After the CRISPR-babies scandal, Qiu openly condemned He’s reckless behavior — only to become embroiled in a comparable scandal himself six years later.

It might be tempting to blame such scandals on individual failings. The deeper questions are: What systemic factors shaped their behavior? What does the incident reveal about China’s Achilles heel in biotechnology—and about the broader culture of international science in which it is embedded? And what can the lessons teach clinical research worldwide?

Fatal Flaw

It would be unfair to suggest that China hasn’t tried to strengthen its ethical governance. The CRISPR-babies scandal prompted deep soul-searching among Chinese scholars and government officials. Since then, President Xi Jinping reportedly championed an “ethics first” approach, contrasting the “science first” mindset often seen in Chinese research. New measures have included incorporating ethics provisions in China’s first Civil Law Code, creating a national ethics committee , and enacting new ethics-review guidelines for clinical research.

But powerful forces are also pushing in the opposite direction. In 2016, China launched Healthy China 2030, making rapid application of emerging medical technologies in clinical practice a priority — not only to address unmet medical needs but to boost national competitiveness. Reforms created a new pathway to translate basic research into clinical applications for cutting-edge technologies overseen by the health ministry, alongside the conventional drug-approval route regulated by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), China’s equivalent of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This became widely known as the dual-track regulatory system.

“Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies.”

Under the technology track, clinical trials are often initiated by university researchers working with hospital clinicians rather than companies. Such investigator-initiated trials (IITs) exist worldwide. Until new regulations took effect this May, Chinese IITs were distinctive in that they could proceed with hospital approvals without the national regulatory oversight required for conventional drug trials. Compared with the NMPA route, the faster pathway allowed researchers to assess promising technologies in humans more quickly and at lower costs and help attract investment.

The result was a boom in IITs. By one estimate , more than 40,000 had been registered by April 2026, involving hundreds of thousands of participants and accounting for much of China’s translational research aimed at applying basic research to clinical practice.

China’s IIT model attracted worldwide attention. Kiran Musunuru, an expert on gene therapy at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, told me that “there is a widespread perception” that Chinese-style IITs offer a way to conduct first-in-human trials quickly and inexpensively. U.S. companies are increasingly interested in conducting IITs in China. Some U.S. researchers have even argued that the U.S should adopt elements of China’s model to accelerate drug discovery and enhance its competitiveness.

Critics, however, point to a fatal flaw: quality control. Driven by the pursuit of high-impact papers— whether for career advancement or hospital rankings — researchers rushed into first-in-human trials of emerging technologies. Hospitals are overwhelmed by proposals involving technologies with varying levels of risk. Researchers told me that as many as two dozen applications can be assessed in a single afternoon. In many cases, the process has become “a rubber-stamping exercise,” explained Zhu Wei, a bioethicist at the Shanghai Clinical Research Center.

A recent analysis of Chinese stem-cell IITs found that although a small fraction helped accelerate the application of basic research to clinical practice, most were repetitive, lacked innovation and wasted resources. Musunuru — who led the landmark development of a personalized gene-editing trial for Baby KJ, an infant with a rare life-threatening deficiency of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 that can cause dangerous ammonia buildup in the blood — warns that allowing individual hospitals to approve first-in-human trials of emerging technologies is particularly dangerous, because few researchers have sufficient experience to assess their risks. They would be “operating blind,” he told me, leaving the outcome dependent on “their appetite for risk.” That appetite can be amplified by institutional conflicts of interest. Successful trials of emerging technologies can bring researchers and hospitals fame, career advancement, high rankings and resources. Jing-Bao Nie, a bioethicist at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, told me that these incentives can undermine institutional judgment and jeopardize patient safety. In Mei’s case, he noted, the lure of a “world-class breakthrough” may have overwhelmed necessary caution. Political interference, which is common in China, is another way the appetite for risk may outweigh caution. Chinese researchers told me that senior hospital leaders often chair the committees that review trial applications. When they seek to push through major projects led by prominent scientists, other committee members may feel unable to object. Read Noema in print. A central regulator is more insulated from such pressures and can also draw on a far broader pool of expertise. As Musumuru notes, the FDA has an army of experienced reviewers who have assessed successful and failed trials, as well as those involving serious adverse effects. Its decisions are therefore informed by “the widest possible body of knowledge,” he told me. “That’s very reassuring.” Oversight Deficiencies Zhai Xiaomei, a bioethicist at the Peking Union Medical College and a member of the national science and technology ethics committee, was not wrong when she told New Beijing News that the problems exposed by Mei’s tragedy had improved since China’s State Council Order No. 818, which established a new regulatory framework for clinical research and commercial application of cutting-edge biomedical technologies, took effect this May. Under the new rules, only top-tier hospitals can undertake IITs. Trials involving emerging technologies like gene and cell therapy, brain-machine interfaces, transplantation and microbial therapies must undergo further review by the health ministry after hospital approval. Adverse effects must be reported within five working days. Violations can result in fines, suspension or permanent ban on clinical research, loss of licenses and even criminal charges. The scientific community in China and abroad welcomes the new rules. But a researcher working closely with the ministry, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to potential career repercussions, told me that it lacks sufficient staff with the necessary technical expertise to review the large volume of applications. Consequently, the researcher added, the reviews rely heavily on experts from universities and hospitals, with only a handful assessing each case. By contrast, Musunuru told me that the U.S. FDA employs numerous in-house reviewers, many with decades of experience, and dozens pore over each submission. If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, he argues, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality. “If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality.” More troublingly, Order 818 lacks mechanisms to monitor what happens locally and identify violations. It includes neither an inspection process — a crucial component of regulatory oversight in countries such as the U.S. and UK — nor a whistleblowing platform for reporting adverse effects and deaths. Such mechanisms are particularly important in countries where transparency is limited, and the press is not free. Without them, violations may go unnoticed and the penalties risk becoming little more than empty threats. Researchers, like bioethicist Ma Yonghui of Xiamen University, also worry that regulatory exemptions could create loopholes. Military hospitals, for instance, fall outside health ministry rules. The two dozen or so free trade zones across China, particularly in Bo’ao on the tropical island of Hainan, may enjoy special regulatory treatment, potentially attracting foreign researchers and companies seeking to conduct ethically contentious trials they could not undertake in their own countries. There are ample precedents of scientists exploiting countries with weak ethics governance as sites for risky research. In October 2018, one month before the CRISPR-babies scandal, He and John Zhang, founder and medical director of the New Hope Fertility Center in New York City, met Hainan’s vice governor to discuss establishing a clinic in Bo’ao to offer experimental procedures, including heritable genome editing. Zhang had already attracted international attention in 2016 for helping produce in Mexico the world’s first “three-parent baby” to prevent the transmission of mitochondrial DNA mutations from the mother. The procedure involved replacing faulty mitochondria with healthy ones from a female donor during in vitro fertilization, a procedure that was — and still is — illegal in the U.S. Hype & Hope While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations, Nie told me. The case offers a window into people’s relationship with biotechnology in China as well as their hopes and expectations — shaped not only by scientists but by society at large. Over the past decade, rare-disease advocacy organizations have grown rapidly in China, helping improve patient care, pressing for government support and driving research through collecting genetic data, studying disease progression and funding clinical trials. Su Yeyang, an independent anthropologist in Langfang in Hebei province who works with rare-disease communities, told me this has given families a sense of agency. With limited social support and a market-driven drug-discovery model that has failed rare-disease communities worldwide, they are doing whatever they can “to help themselves, their children and their community,” she said. With gene therapy, the “magic cure” long hoped for by many rare-disease patients seems within reach. In one high-profile case, a fledgling company approached Xu Wei, a high-school graduate in his 30s in Kunming, in China’s southern province of Yunnan, to develop a gene therapy for his son. The boy had Menkes syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that impairs copper absorption and causes developmental delays and premature death. The company, with no track record in neurodevelopmental diseases, claimed to have developed the treatment in less than a year. In 2022, the 3-year-old received it at a private hospital in a trial that, based on publicly available accounts, appeared not to include biomarker or behavioral assessments of efficacy. Chinese media reported enthusiastically on anecdotal claims of improvements while downplaying the risks of undertaking such experimental therapies. A patient advocacy leader told me such cases are not uncommon in China, where at least 20 million people are living with rare diseases. They offer hope, whether grounded in evidence or not, and can encourage others to follow. “We try to explain to families that pouring millions into a trial is no guarantee of success” and could even backfire, she says. Even well-educated parents, like Mei’s, may underestimate the complexity of clinical research and overestimate what experimental therapies can achieve. It’s unclear whether Qiu, who was fired by the university last week and barred from participating in scientific research for five years following the government investigation , helped foster such expectations. He has not publicly given his account. But his book, “ The Autism Enlightenment ,” published this April, was revealing. It recounted how, in 2010, he told the mother of a child with Rett syndrome — a rare, genetic neurodevelopmental disorder leading to severe cognitive and physical impairments — that a cure would likely emerge in three to five years. It did not discuss fatal risks often associated with first-in-human trials. It did not mention Jessie Gelsinger, who had a mild form of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, a condition that can lead to abnormally high levels of ammonia in the blood and died in 1999 from a preventable complication of an experimental gene therapy. “While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations.” Gelsinger was the first person publicly identified as having died in a gene therapy clinical trial, which undermined public trust in the field and set back its progress for decades. Nor did the book draw caution from the death in 2024 of a girl with Rett syndrome in the first brain-directed gene therapy for the condition. In both cases, scientists used the same type of virus as Qiu did. In a society where disability and genetic disease remain stigmatized, and families receive limited support, Mei’s parents placed their hopes in Qiu and gene editing. Like the couple who turned to He Jiankui to protect their children from HIV and the associated discrimination by editing their embryos, they sought a technological solution to social problems. As the Illness Challenge Foundation, a Beijing-based rare-disease advocacy organization, put it after Mei’s death , “responsible innovation should not entice patients to stake their lives in the name of hope.” China’s Gelsinger Moment? Gelsinger’s death in 1999 was a game changer. It’s widely regarded as a cautionary tale of how a toxic combination of scientific hype and insufficient safeguards can jeopardize patient safety. It triggered institutional reforms and significant changes in research culture in the U.S. that were aimed at rebuilding public and regulatory trust. Mei’s death could be China’s Gelsinger moment. It has exposed regulatory failings, a scientific ethos that encourages hype and recklessness, and deeper societal problems surrounding disability and genetic disease. None is unique to China, but they are particularly acute in a country facing a distinctive combination of political and developmental challenges. At the heart of the incident lies the “moral arbitrage” of experimental therapies, a recurrent theme in biotechnological innovation worldwide. On one hand, patients want access to cutting-edge, unproven treatments when they see them as their only hope. On the other hand, such treatments carry risks, which often accompany medical breakthroughs. Navigating the contours between hope and risk requires more than scientific evidence and regulatory rules, Su told me. It demands critical reflection on the culture of international science that places a premium on competition, sensational research, and being first at any cost. It also calls for broader societal dialogues about the diverse notions of human flourishing, the stigmatization of disabilities, and the need for greater support for people living with rare diseases. If China can learn from the failures and undertake the regulatory, scientific and social reforms needed to address its biotech governance failures — and if the rest of the world can look beyond the country’s small number of success stories out of a hidden ocean of low-quality and potentially harmful clinical trials — Mei’s death will not have been in vain. stories.title: Nearly 100 Labour MPs including ministerial aides oppose Rosebank oil field
stories.summary: Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is due to make a decision on whether to give the go-ahead for drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland within weeks.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 26 November 2026

Ministerial aides are among nearly 100 Labour MPs who have signed a letter to the prime minister to express their opposition to the Rosebank oil field.

The government could also face resignations from junior ranks if the project goes ahead, the BBC has been told.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is due to make a decision on whether to give the go-ahead for drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland within weeks.

The government has remained tight-lipped - both publicly and privately - about what it is likely to do.

Those close to the energy secretary insist that she has not yet made her decision.

But 92 Labour MPs have signed a letter, sent to the prime minister today, urging him not to allow the project to go ahead. Ministerial aides - the most junior rank of government - are among the signatures.

The MP who organised the letter, Catherine Fookes, said: "If Rosebank is approved, champagne corks will pop in the offices of oil companies - but it will not make an iota of difference to my constituents' energy bills.

"The oil belongs to private companies, and will only be shipped overseas to the highest bidder.

"What it will do, however, is accelerate the climate crisis, which is already pushing up food bills, causing devastating winter floods like those we saw in Monmouthshire last year, and fuelling wildfires across our green landscapes in summer."

It's the most visible demonstration yet of the deep divides in the Labour Party over the issue.

The decision about whether to approve Rosebank involves a legal process which technically lies solely with the energy secretary.

Fahnbulleh has, in the past, been regarded as someone personally opposed to the oil field.

Others in the cabinet, including Chancellor John Healey, have let it be known that they would like to see the project given the go-ahead; while the prime minister has repeatedly said he wants to take a "pragmatic" approach to North Sea oil and gas.

But Fahnbulleh insisted last month that she alone would make the final decision and claimed the courts would ultimately side with her if colleagues attempted to overrule her.

Influential pro-Rosebank voices suggested that senior ministers had toned down vocal support as the decision draws closer.

They suggested this wasn't a sign that Rosebank would be vetoed, but because any obvious attempts to pressure the energy secretary might mean her final decision would be subject to a legal challenge.

Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander (left) and Chancellor John Healey (right) accompany Miatta Fahnbulleh on a visit to a Shell gas terminal

A number of MPs say they have heard conflicting claims - with both outcomes being predicted.

What is clearer is that the government's decision will be controversial, whichever way it goes. There is a private and public battle playing out.

Backers of the scheme argue approving it would provide an economic boost. The Conservatives also say it would enhance energy security.

But oil is traded internationally – and the energy secretary has said approving the scheme will not help with immediate cost of living pressures. Rosebank would also be more polluting than Jackdaw, a gas field, which was approved last month.

A fortnight ago, backers of the field were confident it would be approved.

They believed the chancellor's language on energy bills at the Budget , coupled with the lack of political jeopardy that materialised from the approval of the Jackdaw gas field, had made their case stronger.

The same group of MPs believe it would be difficult to reject Rosebank around the same time the prime minister is set to deliver a 10-year plan focused on reindustrialisation.

The government has said oil and gas would be part of the energy mix for many years to come and sources in the trade union movement have suggested that if Rosebank doesn't go ahead, existing inward investment in the North Sea would be put at risk.

While Labour's manifesto upon entering power in 2024 pledged not to "issue new licences to explore new fields", it does pledge to honour existing ones.

In 2023, the then Conservative UK government granted a licence for Rosebank and a legal challenge followed.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approval unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a new decision on whether to give the go-ahead.

The mood among some pro-Rosebank MPs changed this week, with several who back approval telling the BBC they were now worried it would be blocked.

The BBC has spoken privately to Labour MPs involved in the debate, before the letter was sent to the prime minister, to get a sense of how divisive it is proving.

One ministerial aide said: "There are quite a few of us who are considering our positions. I'm in that group. We want to see leadership on climate change."

Another aide who said they might quit added: "There a group of us for whom we became Labour MPs because of climate change. It is the issue that motivated us into politics."

Other aides – known in Westminster as parliamentary private secretaries – told the BBC they were opposed, but would stay in their jobs if it went ahead.

Another said they thought there were increasing signs the prime minister would not be able to carry his party with him if the scheme was given the thumbs up.

And another said the energy secretary might have to resign if it goes ahead, given her scepticism about the project.

It has been reported in recent weeks that members of her team are encouraging opponents to make their feelings known. The BBC has been told the same.

One MP, who backs Rosebank, said the behind-the-scenes operation had been so effective, the scheme was up in the air again.

That has led to some anger at the energy secretary.

One minister says: "Miatta has boxed herself in with how she's handled Rosebank. It's outrageous if she's encouraging MPs to speak up over Rosebank. We should get on and do it."

Like the decision itself, the exact timeframe is unclear. But some opposition figures expect it mid-December.

Whatever happens, it will be controversial and has already exposed splits in the Labour Party.

stories.title: Mandelson kept shares as ambassador despite conflict of interest fears, documents show
stories.summary: The peer was sacked as ambassador last year over his relationship with the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 26 November 2026

Lord Mandelson still held shares in his lobbying company eight months after becoming US ambassador, despite government concens about conflicts of interest, newly released documents show.

The peer was sacked as ambassador last year by Sir Keir Starmer following revelations about the extent of his relationship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

This 85-page release is the third since MPs voted to publish documents aiming to reveal behind-the scenes-discussions about how he was appointed to the role.

The documents were previously withheld due to the Metropolitan Police investigation into allegations Lord Mandelson had passed market-sensitive government information to Epstein.

Sir Olly Robbins was sacked as head of the Foreign Office by Sir Keir Starmer during the scandal when it emerged Lord Mandelson had been granted clearance for the role despite concerns being raised by vetting officials.

The newly released documents highlight that Lord Mandelson was able to keep his shares in Global Counsel, the lobbying company he co-founded, while serving as ambassador to Washington.

They reveal civil servants' concerns about the risk of perceived conflict of interest.

But selling the shares was clearly not a condition of him taking up the role.

Part of that is because of the desire in Sir Keir's government at the time to have Lord Mandelson in Washington as quickly as possible.

That is exemplified in an email from Sir Olly, saying a process to police Mandelson's conflicts of interest could be "up and running in a light touch way".

Another factor is selling shares in a private company like Global Counsel, which advised high-profile clients including Chinese-owned TikTok, US tech firm Palantir and pharmaceutical firm GSK. requires finding a new buyer or selling them back to the company.

But the documents also reveal Lord Mandelson had not sold his shares back to Global Counsel because their offer was not the "fair value". Another attempt to sell to a different buyer fell through.

The result was Mandelson kept his shares, and while in office tried to set up a meeting between Global Counsel and a key Donald Trump advisor, as well as taking the firm's advice on a speech on Britain's role in the world.

Lord Mandelson remained a shareholder until February 2026 , the same month the company went into administration.

Sir Olly wrote to David Lammy in August to tell him Lord Mandelson still had not divested himself of his Global Counsel shares

Emails about his dealings with his Washington counterparts show a close relationship, with one message from an unnamed White House official in April 2025 telling Lord Mandelson his label as the "Prince of Darkness" could not be "farther from the truth".

Ahead of a speech he was due to give on Britain's role "in the age of Trump", documents show him seeking advice from a Global Counsel employee in August 2025, during his time as ambassador.

The exchange contains feedback from an unnamed Global Counsel director, who suggested he should use "warmer language" about China and tone down "parts of your apologia of the Trump administration".

The director warned: "Scepticism of [the Trump administration] is now so deep – at least in the public policy-interested world outside government – that it would be counterproductive/unpersuasive if you came across as having drunk the Kool Aid."

Lord Mandelson responds to say he would water down his language, and in another email tries to arrange an "under the radar" lunch meeting to discuss China and trade between a GC employee and someone from the US President's Council of Economic Advisers.

On the domestic front, Lord Mandelson also sent texts to Sir Keir's then chief of staff Morgan McSweeney in September 2025 offering advice on a cabinet reshuffle.

He suggested moving Darren Jones to lead the science and technology department as a way to "solve your Darren issue", although McSweeney did not respond until after the reshuffle decisions had been made, with Jones given a newly-created role as chief secretary to the prime minister.

Lord Mandelson has yet to comment on the most recent release of papers relating to his appointment.

He has repeatedly let it be known he believes he has not acted criminally, did not act for personal gain and is cooperating with the police.

No charges have been made. A Met Police spokesperson told the BBC: "Our investigation into alleged misconduct in public office is ongoing."

Speaking to journalists in the Downing Street garden following the release of the documents, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would address culture change for Westminster as part of his 10 year plan, which he said will be published next month.

He said: "I've come back in as something of an outsider into the system and I see a lot of things that I think need to change to improve the political culture of this country and to strengthen the public interests when it comes to all of these issues."

Security minister Dan Jarvis told MPs: "The government recognises that action needs to be taken in response to the issues raised by Mandelson's appointment."

He said action had already been taken to strengthen the vetting and appointments process, including strengthening the management of conflicts of interest.

Future appointments will not be made before security clearance has been granted, he said, adding that review by Sir Adrian Fulford of vetting procedures was nearing completion.

A separate review by Sir Anthony Finkelstein into use of personal messaging services including WhatsApp and Signal for business purposes is expected to be published in January next year.
