stories.title: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause
stories.summary: Text of the treaties was published this afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 26 November 2026

The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.

The treaties were published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.

The deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay "reasonable and proportionate costs" to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.

Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal while Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.

The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the future of the UK-EU relationship.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Two of the three legal texts were released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.

A new assessment of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country was also released.

EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme Published 1 day ago

Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students Published 1 day ago

Farage helps launch new campaign against the UK rejoining the EU Published 1 day ago

Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost the export of major agricultural commodities.

The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."

"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."

A plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.

The treaty text also contains finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules. The UK will be invited to attend European Commission meetings and expert groups as an observer, as well as taking part in emergency food security planning.

However, the UK will not be given voting rights.

Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, are detailed in the legislation.

Such powers will enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.

Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week , the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".

Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

stories.title: UK reservists contacted as 'threat environment' rises, Streeting says
stories.summary: It comes after reports that reservists have received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Reservist soldiers training at Longmoor camp in southern England in 2024 (file photo)

Published 26 November 2026

The Ministry of Defence has written to ex-military personnel to check their contact details and skills against the backdrop of a rising "threat environment", Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said.

It comes after The Times and the Telegraph reported that reservists who previously served in the Armed Forces have received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.

Streeting told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that this meant should they ever be needed "either for a national disaster here at home or for a more serious threat or conflict elsewhere" then they would "know where our strategic reserve is" and what their skills were.

"I want the country to be alert, not alarmed," he said.

"You can't not look at what's going on in Europe and not be concerned about a threat environment which has deteriorated in recent years and is sadly increasing," Streeting told Today.

"We saw last Friday a very serious incident – the incursion into Polish airspace by Russian missiles, we've seen state-sponsored terrorism waged by Russia across Europe, we've obviously had incidents concerning Iran around RAF bases here in the UK.

"And so against that backdrop, against that threat environment, the government and the country has to be ready to face down those risks."

He added: "Because the more ready we are the less likely we are to find ourselves in a conflict, in a war, that is my goal, that is the goal of this government."

Streeting told BBC Breakfast that "if, God forbid, this country did find itself at war" and there was then an inquiry, the Ministry of Defence would be criticised if the government had not kept its records up-to-date."

The Telegraph reported that the letters offered opportunities to volunteer , external for training and exercises.

This is not a case of pressing the panic button for imminent war, but more one of good housekeeping.

When Britain went to war in Iraq in 2003 the MoD had a poor grasp of who might be available to serve, what current skills they had and what their up-to-date contact details were. So they obviously don't want to be in that situation if there is a national crisis in the future that triggers a mobilisation.

Twenty three years on, the Ukraine war has changed everything. It's brought a hot war to the very borders of Nato, it's exposed the dangers of having too few troops available, but most of all it has changed the nature of warfare.

People who have spent their adult lives never touching a weapon can turn out to be extraordinarily skilled drone operators, those with a talent for electronics, radio and signals work have a vital role to play in electronic warfare.

So this exercise by the government, probably long overdue, is about knowing who can do what and where they can be contacted.

Justin Crump, a former Army officer and now CEO of the business intelligence firm Sibylline, told the BBC: "Ukraine has shown us the importance of mobilising civilian skills and approaches in modern warfare. This is a first step, and an overdue one in many ways, with the effort likely to increase through early 2027. [It is] very much a part of deterrence and not an intention to use people".

He said veterans - a sometimes misleading term for men and women who are often in peak physical shape and fitness - that he has contacted have generally responded positively to the move. "After all", he said, "they signed up to help before, but want to make sure their enhanced skills and talents are valued".

The MoD's decision to contact ex-military personnel comes after news that the UK has signed an £8bn contract to upgrade its nuclear submarine fleet, which the defence secretary said would help get the country "warfighting ready".

Meanwhile, Streeting also praised the Duke of Sussex's "patriotic spirit" after the former Army officer said he would rejoin the armed forces again if needed.

Asked whether there could be a role for Harry, the defence secretary told Today: "I'm always happy to talk to him about how we can work together, whether that's through his Invictus Games, which does a brilliant job supporting our veterans and giving them opportunities to take part in those amazing and inspiring competitive sporting events, but he does have experience to bring to bear."

Streeting praised the "service he's given to our country" and the fact he had spoken about his "willingness and readiness to serve".

"I think that's exactly the sort of patriotic spirit we're looking for," he said.

"I think it's that sort of patriotic spirit we'll find throughout our strategic reserve."

Last week, Harry, who spent a decade in the forces and served on the front line in Afghanistan, said: "If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country, alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel."

stories.title: Ministers hiding behind data protection on Sir Galahad bombing files, says veteran
stories.summary: Falklands veterans demand UK government release more files from 1982 inquiry.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Forty-eight were killed when Sir Galahad was attacked in 1982.

Published 26 November 2026

A Falklands War veteran who was left severely burned in an attack on his ship has accused ministers of hiding behind data protection in refusing to release all files on the bombing.

The undefended supply ship Sir Galahad was hit by Argentinian planes in June 1982m killing 48 people, including 32 Welsh Guards.

The Welsh Guards had previously been blamed for not leaving the ship earlier, but files released later cleared them of any blame .

Simon Weston said veterans "just want to know who is responsible for making terrible decisions".

The UK government said it had to strike a balance between respecting legal obligations and giving veterans the answers they needed.

A 1982 Royal Navy inquiry was held in private and its findings unreleased.

Excerpts have been released over time, including in 2024, when two files were released.

But five files comprising 308 witness statements are closed and, under the terms of the Public Records Act 1958, are not due to be released until 2065.

More than 100 were injured in the bombing. Another eight died on the Sir Tristram while dozens of others were injured.

Weston, and fellow veteran Mike Hermanis, attended a Commons debate on the management and disclosure of records from the inquiry on Wednesday.

'We're not interested in anything but the truth'

Weston, 65, a former Welsh guardsman, said he was "disappointed" by the response.

He said ministers must "stop hiding behind GDPR", referring to the regulations that have governed data protection since the 2010s.

"It wasn't meant for what went on in '82 and statements that were made in '82. So we feel that people will be hiding behind a law that wasn't theirs to hide behind," he said.

"We're not interested in anything other than the truth. We just want to know who is responsible for making terrible decisions."

The scheduled release date was too late to help anyone, he said.

"We'll all be dead by then and it benefits not us or the families.

"It's been a terrible tortuous 44 years and some of the families have passed away since then, sisters and brothers of the bereaved, and it's just not fair on them."

Simon Weston accuses ministers of hiding behind data protection regulation

Hermanis, 64, from Newport, was on board the ship as a 19-year-old guardsman.

He said ministers' refusal to unseal files until 2065 was "very deflating".

"After being there for 90 minutes and at the 11th hour, that was a sledgehammer blow to us.

"But we've been campaigning for 44 years, so we'll just keep on going, keep knocking, somebody's going to open our door."

He said watching the debate had been "overwhelming" and he was moved to tears by the amount of support from backbench MPs.

"These MPs, they're all different parties, and they came together to give us truth, justice and transparency. That's all we want: honesty."

Transcripts 'missing from the record'

Labour's Newport East MP, Dame Jessica Morden, secured the debate after being contacted about the issue by Hermanis, who is her constituent.

Morden also said ministers had confirmed to her that some of the transcripts and tape recordings of key witnesses given as part of an inquiry into the bombing were "missing from the record, having somehow been lost at an unknown point over the years".

"It is really hard to see, 40 years later, how the current approach can be justified," she told MPs.

The former Conservative leader Iain Duncan Smith, who served in the Scots Guards, said it was "shameful" the Welsh Guards had been blamed when those above them had made mistakes.

Chris Evans, the Labour MP for Caerphilly, said he was "utterly disgusted" the Welsh Guards had been blamed for the tragedy, and said the UK government had a "chance to put that right".

The minister for the armed forces, Louise Sandher-Jones, said she wanted to be clear the Welsh Guards were not at fault.

"The Welsh Guards were absolutely not to blame in any way. In fact, as we have heard, they showed amazing bravery and heroism with their actions that day," she told MPs.

But she said ministers had legal obligations they must respect.

"Section 40 of the Freedom of Information Act protects the personal information of living individuals. That is why those files currently should remain closed until 2065. There are also obligations under the Data Protection Act 2018," she told MPs.

Sandher-Jones also said it was important to consider carefully "whether the wider impact of releasing reports to do with a historical event means that, in some future tragedy, we constrain being able to get to the truth".

stories.title: Heathrow third runway plans 'should be grounded'
stories.summary: The runway plans do not fully address issues including climate tests, the Transport Committee says.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
An artist's impression showing three runways at Heathrow Airport

Published 26 November 2026

The government has "failed to make the case" for Heathrow Airport's expansion, the chair of the Transport Committee has said, as a highly anticipated report on the £33bn project is published.

Ruth Cadbury said the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement did not adequately address noise, air pollution and climate tests.

"Plans for a third runway should be grounded for now and the government should go back to the drawing board," she said.

Downing Street has repeatedly said the prime minister would wait for the Transport Committee's report, among other factors, before deciding whether to back the scheme. The prime minister's office has been contacted for comment.

What's the plan for a third runway at Heathrow Airport? Published 30 January 2025

The report said the climate test was examined in the context of the recent advice from the Climate Change Committee.

The results showed the west London airport's expansion would not be compatible with the UK's carbon budgets or net-zero targets, it said.

The committee said both the air quality test and the noise test should be strengthened, adding that there was a lack of certainty over the cost of expansion that could affect the prices paid by airlines and passengers.

It also raised concerns over a lack of extensive plans to improve public transport, such as new rail lines into Heathrow from the west and south.

"If a third runway is to get off the ground, then government also needs to strengthen the air quality test and noise tests, develop plans for improving public transport and bottom out how much it will cost airlines and passengers to use an expanded Heathrow," Cadbury said.

She also called for "robust analysis" to set out what would happen if decarbonisation goals were missed.

"Expansion should not go ahead at any price, or at any cost to society or the environment," the report said.

'Weight of evidence'

A spokesperson for the Department for Transport said the government had made clear that Heathrow expansion could only go ahead if it met four tests covering economic growth, climate change, noise and air quality.

They added: "We note the findings from the committee's report and will consider these as we continue to review responses to our consultation on the policy framework underpinning expansion."

Ruth Cadbury's west London constituency is close to Heathrow Airport

Paul McGuinness, chair of the No 3rd Runway Coalition group, said the expansion would "leave the country worse off, once the negative costs are taken into account".

However, Heathrow's chief executive Thomas Woldbye said the "overwhelming weight of evidence and support remains strongly behind Heathrow expansion".

"Successive governments, independent commissions and industry experts have repeatedly concluded that you either expand Heathrow so the UK can compete and grow, or you accept a steady erosion of the UK's connectivity and global competitiveness," he said.

Cadbury, Labour MP for Brentford and Isleworth in west London, has been outspoken about her opposition to the expansion .

Lord Khan, who was the MP for Tooting before becoming London mayor in 2016, also opposes a third runway .

He previously told BBC Radio London that noise, air pollution and climate change targets were his main concerns.

Then-chancellor Rachel Reeves announced last year the government was backing the scheme .

She previously said it would add 0.5% to the UK's GDP, although updated government forecasts in June recalibrated this figure at just 0.05%.

'100,000 jobs'

The Transport Committee's report said the government had positioned expansion as "critical" to national growth, but that "the case for this designation applying to Heathrow expansion has not been made".

Heathrow is the UK's busiest airport, serving more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways.

The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average - if a third runway is built.

It is estimated the project would create 100,000 jobs.

But it would see homes demolished, rivers diverted and the M25 motorway rerouted through a tunnel between junctions 14 and 15.

The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested a date of 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues.

Administration is suggesting an added 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total to about 40%

US politics live – latest updates

Donald Trump is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the European Union, that would go into effect early next year, the office of the US trade representative said on Wednesday.

The administration is proposing an additional 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total tax to about 40%. Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

In February, the supreme court ruled Trump’s so-called Liberation Day tariffs illegal. The court issued a narrow decision saying the administration had improperly used a specific emergency powers law to implement the tariffs, but did not broadly curb the president’s power to introduce new tariffs.

The administration is now using section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 as the legal basis for the new rounds of tariffs. The law gives the executive branch power to respond to unfair foreign trade practices after conducting formal investigations.

Though the White House did not give a timeline for the new tariffs, it said they could go into effect in January at the earliest. The US trade office said it would hold hearings on the new tariffs and its investigation into the unfair trade practices on 25 January.

This is the second major batch of section 301 tariffs, after the White House announced a broad slate of tariffs on more than 80 countries in July, including the UK, Mexico and Canada, saying the countries had failed to enforce bans on forced labor. A lawsuit fighting those tariffs is currently awaiting a decision in the court of international trade.

“For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America’s manufacturing base,” the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, said in a statement on Wednesday.

“President Trump is proposing to take action to bring about the elimination of these unfair acts, policies, and practices. In doing so, we can level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.”

Tariffs have proven unpopular with US voters, who handed Democrats a decisive victory in the midterm elections that will give the party control of Congress. The Yale Budget Lab estimates that tariffs currently in effect have added an additional $900 annually in costs for each US household.

The rising cost of living was the number one issue for voters ahead of November’s midterm elections, according to a Harris Poll survey for the Guardian. An earlier Harris poll found seven in 10 Americans blamed tariffs for higher prices.

Consumer prices rose an annualized 3.8% in October, the Bureau of Economic Analysis announced on Wednesday, the highest rate since May and well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% annual target.

stories.title: Burnham caught in north-south satellite deal battle
stories.summary: North East MPs want a planned defence base to be built in Sedgefield.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The decision on where to build Britain's military satellites could fall to the prime minister

Published 26 November 2026

Britain is about to decide who should build a new generation of military satellites that will be vital for our armed forces in any future war.

But the contest between the two remaining rival bidders seems to have embroiled Andy Burnham's government in a home-grown north-south conflict about where the jobs and investment should go.

And MPs and local political leaders in north-east England see it as a test about just how serious the prime minister is about meeting his goal of "growth in every postcode".

Lockheed Martin wants to bring the work on the government's Skynet 6 programme to a new £85m factory in County Durham - and the site at NetPark in Sedgefield is in an area which certainly needs the 500 jobs being promised.

But supporters of rival bidder Airbus have said that will come at a huge cost in jobs at the company's sites in Portsmouth and Stevenage in the south and east of England.

And like many battles, this one has posed a challenge in sifting propaganda from truth.

At its heart is a vital decision. These satellites will be crucial to UK national security as they will carry encrypted secret communications for our armed forces.

With space now becoming increasingly militarised and a potential theatre of war, it will be vital they are as safe as possible from attack.

The government began the bidding process for the £2bn contract in May 2023, but as a decision has got closer, the contest has become more intense.

Officially the two remaining companies still in the race, Lockheed Martin and Airbus, cannot advocate publicly for their respective bids.

Gunning hard

But there is a proxy war being fought, with competing arguments emerging from rival camps.

The North East's politicians are unsurprisingly gunning hard for Lockheed Martin and none harder than MP Alan Strickland, as the site would be in his Newton Aycliffe and Spennymoor constituency.

He has pointed to the growing number of North East firms working in the space sector as evidence the region can deliver.

A centre dedicated to the industry is also soon to open at Northumbria University in Newcastle, partly funded by £15m from Lockheed Martin.

The North East Space Skills and Technology Centre (Nesst) could provide vital research capacity and a flow of graduates for the industry.

County Durham Labour MP Alan Strickland has said Sedgefield is the right place to site a satellite factory

But Strickland and other North East MPs have also pointed to a lack of defence investment in a region which has historically been one of the strongest recruiting grounds for the armed forces.

According to the latest government figures, while the Ministry of Defence (ModD) invested almost £8.5bn in industry in the South East of England last year, it only invested £200m in the North East. That was lower per head of population than any other part of the UK

Strickland said: "We've got a proud military heritage in our region but despite that we get less than 1% of all MoD spending.

"We feel as North East MPs we can do better. This satellite contract is a real opportunity to invest in the region, creating jobs and opportunities and making sure we have genuinely got growth in every postcode."

But in recent weeks the trade union Unite has been dialling up its own rhetoric on behalf of its members working at Airbus's factories in Portsmouth and Stevenage.

Unite's Peter Hughes has said thousands of jobs are at risk if Airbus fails to win the Skynet 6 contract

Airbus has won previous UK military satellite contracts and the union has said losing out could cost up to 3,000 jobs at those sites. There is concern in Wales too about the impact on work carried out at sites in Newport and Broughton.

It has also cast doubt on Lockheed Martin's plans for Sedgefield, implying that much of the work might take place in the US, where the company has its headquarters.

The union's general secretary Sharon Graham has said the government could end up "shooting itself in the foot" if it makes the wrong decision.

Unite's head of manufacturing Peter Hughes said: "Is it a promise that's actually going to be delivered?

"At the moment, they haven't even put a spade in the ground to build this factory.

"Are they actually going to be well-paid jobs, or are they just going to be assembly jobs, not specialised posts in research and development?

"It's important jobs are in the North East but not if it means getting one job in the North East means losing five jobs elsewhere. That doesn't make sense."

Lockheed Martin wants to make military satellites as part of the government's Skynet 6 programme at NETpark in Sedgefield

Unite has also questioned the wisdom of handing such a sensitive contract to a company whose ultimate headquarters is in the US.

It has raised the spectre of recent events in Ukraine where the country's armed forces have been hindered in their battle against Russia by l imits on their access to parts of the Starlink satellite system developed by Elon Musk.

This is scaremongering, according to supporters of Lockheed Martin who have said the contract would leave complete control over the satellites with the UK government, with no possibility of US interference.

They have also cast doubt on the potential jobs impact.

Lockeed's backers have also said preparatory work on access has already begun at the Sedgefield site and it could be up and running within two years, rather than the five years Unite have suggested it could take to build the factory.

The company has also already supplied the UK with vital and sensitive defence equipment that includes the RAF's F-35 fighter jets.

A Lockheed Martin spokesman said it could not comment on the procurement process.

"Lockheed Martin UK, a British company, will establish facilities to develop an ecosystem alongside our regional partners in the North East of England to provide the UK with a sovereign space capability," they said.

"It will create jobs, supply chain opportunities, and the potential for exports. It will have a UK Design Authority and a UK Chief Engineer."

An Airbus spokesman said: ""Airbus remains fully committed to the Skynet competition and we continue to comply with all requirements and timelines set by the Ministry of Defence."

Lockheed Martin has already supplied the UK with F-35 Lightning fighters

Unite's lobbying might be having an effect. A decision on the contract has been delayed.

All a MoD spokesperson would say for now is: "This is an ongoing procurement process, and no final decisions have been made."

But it is a decision with political consequences. Airbus's sites in Portsmouth and Stevenage are in constituencies Labour took in 2024 that will be targeted by the Conservatives at the next election.

And Labour's political challengers in County Durham are watching carefully too.

Reform UK took control of the county council in 2024 and its deputy leader Darren Grimes said this is a test for the prime minister.

"Andy Burnham promised a Makerfield test from within 10 Downing Street - the places that Westminster have neglected would finally get some semblance of fairness.

"I think this is the golden opportunity.

"I do think the people of County Durham would wonder why he was going back on promises he made, and it would allow the North East once more to feel it is the forgotten part of the country."

A decision might come before the end of the year, but in this battle over military hardware, Andy Burnham could face a no-win scenario in choosing between north and south.

stories.title: Government's antisemitism adviser launches investigation into BBC
stories.summary: Lord Mann says he has launched the investigation after "growing discomfort among Jewish BBC staff".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The BBC said it is "determined to ensure the BBC is a place where everyone can be themselves and feel accepted"

Published 26 November 2026

The government's antisemitism adviser has launched an investigation into the BBC over allegations of a "hostile work environment" for Jews.

Lord Mann told BBC Radio 4's Today programme he had decided to open the investigation "because there seems to be a growing feeling of discomfort among Jewish staff".

He said: "If that's true, and that's what I'm going to attempt to find out, and if that is widespread, then that's a really serious problem that has to be addressed. And I don't hear and see that being addressed, and at a senior level."

The BBC said it takes "any and all allegations of discrimination extremely seriously – there is no place for it at the BBC".

The corporation said it had introduced compulsory antisemitism training for all staff, and said "we actively encourage colleagues to report any incidences or concerns they have".

The BBC statement added that it is "determined to ensure the BBC is a place where everyone can be themselves and feel accepted".

The Department for Culture, Media and Sport told the BBC: "This government will not tolerate antisemitism. It has no place in our society.

"The BBC has a crucial role in ensuring all communities are heard and feel valued as part of our public life. That is the standard that we expect the BBC to be held to. We will consider Lord Mann's independent report carefully when we receive it."

Lord Mann, who was appointed by former Prime Minister Theresa May as an independent adviser on antisemitism in 2019 , external , said anyone contacting him would have "total anonymity guaranteed".

"I have no agenda against the BBC," he told Today, calling himself "an entirely blank sheet of paper".

"Some of the things that I'm being told have been quite disturbing sometimes, how little the senior manager of the BBC seem to get it, and so I'm opening this up," he said.

"Look, there is a problem. The question is - is the problem just a few people? Is it a problem that's easily solved? But if it's an institutional problem, that's much deeper and more difficult to solve. It may be. I'll report the facts."

The former MP said he had previously "made suggestions" to the corporation after he had "repeatedly met" Jewish staff.

He said the things "the BBC has done to try and sort things out have not worked".

His agenda was "ensuring the BBC meets its charter obligations", saying "people are fearful... of expressing their concerns internally, that's the problem".

Lord Mann's remit as the government's independent adviser on antisemitism includes "to engage proactively with the Jewish community and institutions".

He said he plans to have his investigation "totally completed and reported to the BBC and the government before Easter".

He previously conducted a review into antisemitism and racism in the NHS , which was commissioned by the health secretary and which reported in June.

The Guardian recently reported , external that BBC deputy director general Rhodri Talfan Davies said he did not accept that an independent inquiry into antisemitism was needed.

"We have very, very robust processes – we review them regularly," he told members of the Broadcasting Press Guild earlier this month.

"Of course in any large organisation there can be instances of discrimination, which you deal with when they arise, but there is no evidence of any systemic issue within the BBC that would merit anything like that.

"I don't believe there is institutional discrimination of any sort in the BBC, but I think as an organisation you always have to look harder and review how you go about identifying issues, and that work is never done."

The Board of Deputies of British Jews said in a statement that it welcomed the review into "deeply concerning" experiences of Jewish staff at the BBC.

"The BBC is an important national institution and should be setting the gold standard for an inclusive workplace and impartial broadcasting," it said.

"We stand ready to support both Lord Mann and the BBC in addressing these concerns, rebuilding confidence within the Jewish community and ensuring that the BBC sets an example for other broadcasters to follow."

Last month, Oscar-winning producer Lucie Kon said the BBC had given her a £400,000 payout after she raised antisemitism concerns.

The BBC said it did not uphold allegations of antisemitism but accepted there were "shortcomings" in how it treated Kon, which had a "personal impact" on her. The corporation did not specify what the shortcomings were.

In January, the BBC apologised for its use of language during coverage of Holocaust Memorial Day, saying programmes should have referred to "six million Jewish people" having been murdered by the Nazi regime, rather than "six million people" or "six million mostly Jewish people".

Last September, the BBC's broadcast of Bob Vylan's controversial set at Glastonbury broke editorial guidelines in relation to harm and offence , with the corporation's complaints unit ruling that some comments could "fairly be characterised as antisemitic". The band denied being antisemitic.

stories.summary: Sharp rise expected as cost pressures mount, with experts factoring in energy price cap hike and potential impact of El Niño Food price inflation in the UK could hit 5% next year, the Bank of England has said, despite rising less sharply than feared since the onset of the Iran war. The deputy governor Clare Lombardelli told MPs on the cross-party Treasury select committee: “Food price inflation is coming in under what we expected [it] to be, and in fact under what the industry expected it to be.” Continue reading...
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Sharp rise expected as cost pressures mount, with experts factoring in energy price cap hike and potential impact of El Niño

Food price inflation in the UK could hit 5% next year, the Bank of England has said, despite rising less sharply than feared since the onset of the Iran war.

The deputy governor Clare Lombardelli told MPs on the cross-party Treasury select committee: “Food price inflation is coming in under what we expected [it] to be, and in fact under what the industry expected it to be.”

But she said the Bank expected food price inflation to rise sharply from the current level of about 1.3%. “We think that … it will go up to 3 to 5% in the middle of next year. I mean, obviously that’s quite uncertain, but that pressure is there,” Lombardelli said.

Lombardelli was being questioned by MPs alongside other members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC).

The MPC raised interest rates by a quarter-point to 4% at its last meeting earlier this month to tackle above-target inflation, and suggested further action could be necessary.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, said the MPC was also monitoring the potential impact of this year’s unusually large El Niño weather event on future food prices.

“There is uncertainty around this. You know, we still don’t know what the impact of this El Niño effect is going to be, for instance, because it will take time for it to manifest,” he said.

Surging oil and gas prices have pushed up the annual rate of inflation , which hit 3.6% last month, with the cost of petrol and diesel up by more than 33% over the past year.

But so far there have been fewer knock-on effects beyond energy prices. Food inflation has fallen well short of the peak above 17% seen in 2023, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine exacerbated the supply squeeze as the global economy emerged from the Covid-19 pandemic.

Catherine Mann, an external member of the MPC who voted for a half-point increase this month, pointed to fierce competition in the food retail sector as a reason price rises had been constrained.

“We all go shopping ourselves. I can say that Aldi price match in my stores is apparent. Now, it wasn’t apparent four years ago. So that’s, I think, important,” she said.

Oil prices have fallen sharply since the Democratic party’s sweep in the US midterms brought hopes of an end to the Iran conflict, and as alternative sources of supply start to come onstream.

Bailey said if these lower prices continued, they would moderate the Bank’s predictions for UK inflation – which it had expected to peak at almost 5% next year.

“The prices are volatile … if these current prices were to stay what they are, the peak of inflation mechanically would be lower,” he said. However, Bailey and other MPC members underlined that some inflationary pressure for next year is already baked in – pointing to the 26% rise in the price cap for household energy bills due in January as an example.

The two-hour hearing underlined the divisions within the committee. The more dovish Swati Dhingra suggesting she saw this month’s rate rise as a one-off “insurance” measure, while Mann said she feared the MPC had undermined public confidence by failing to move more aggressively.

Dhingra compared the muted impact of rocketing oil and gas prices this year on the wider economy with the effects of the surge in 2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine.

At a similar point in that year, the prices of 70% of goods included in the consumer price index had risen, she said – but just 20% of prices have reacted so far this year.

But Mann pointed out that inflation had now been consistently above the Bank’s 2% target for five years.

“If we let inflation expectations drift away from 2% in the longer term, then monetary policy is going to have to work harder, meaning a higher rate for longer,” she said, adding: “The optimal response is to hike more and sooner.” The MPC’s next rate-setting meeting is on 17 December.

stories.title: Government preparing to publish more Mandelson papers
stories.summary: The peer was sacked as UK ambassador to the US due to his links with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 26 November 2026

Further documents relating to the appointment of Lord Mandelson as US ambassador are expected to be published by the government later today.

Some documents were published earlier this year after MPs voted to compel the government to release them, but others were withheld at the request of the Metropolitan Police, who are investigating the former ambassador.

The Met has since informed the government the documents can be published without prejudicing their investigation.

Lord Mandelson was arrested in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office. He has repeatedly let it be known he believes he has not acted criminally, did not act for personal gain and is cooperating with the police.

The former Labour peer became the British ambassador to the US in February 2025.

But he was sacked in September of that year after Downing Street said new information about the extent of his relationship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein had emerged.

After his sacking, the government - then led by Sir Keir Starmer - was heavily criticised for giving Lord Mandelson the job and in February MPs voted to force the government to publish papers relating to his appointment.

In March, the first batch of files - running to 147 pages - was released. The documents showed Sir Keir was warned that Lord Mandelson's relationship with Epstein posed a "reputational risk" before he was confirmed as US ambassador.

More documents were published in June and they revealed messages between Lord Mandelson and ministers strongly criticising Sir Keir. The 1,500 pages covered communications about Lord Mandelson's appointment to the post.

The Cabinet Office earlier this month confirmed it was preparing to publish more documents. This led to the Conservatives warning that "we still haven't got to the bottom of the Mandelson scandal".

A Met Police spokesperson said: "Our investigation into alleged misconduct in public office is ongoing."

stories.title: UK signs £8bn deal to ensure submarines are 'warfighting ready'
stories.summary: The deal will allow "work around the clock to get our submarines back out to sea" , Wes Streeting says.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 26 November 2026

The UK has signed an £8bn contract to upgrade its nuclear submarine fleet, which Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said would help get the country "warfighting ready".

The five-year deal, awarded to defence firm Babcock, will create 3,000 new jobs and around 2,500 apprentice and graduate roles mainly across Plymouth, Clyde and Bristol, the MoD said.

It will allow the Royal Navy to "work around the clock to get our submarines back out to sea" and see naval base services modernised, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it demonstrated his commitment to "keeping the public safe" and "providing opportunities to "get young people into work".

"We're providing opportunities to get young people into work, to bring jobs to communities in Plymouth, Clyde and beyond, and to boost growth across the UK," the prime minister added.

Streeting said: "We're not going to repeat the mistakes of the past, where investment in our nuclear capability was delayed.

"Even when we have to move funding from other departments, we will prioritise our nuclear deterrent and getting Britain warfighting ready."

Speaking to BBC Breakfast during a visit to HMNB Devonport on Thursday, the defence secretary described the investment as a "win for the Navy… for jobs and the taxpayer."

He said the structure of the contract incentivises Babcock to produce results, adding "the more productive they are, the more they earn but if they fall short, then they don't get paid as much".

Streeting was also asked about reports that 100,000 military reservists who previously served in the armed forces have received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.

"What we're doing today is contacting our strategic reserves to make sure their contact details are up to date and we have those details to hand and this is all part of our readiness picture," he said.

The funding is part of a wider £26bn investment into the UK's naval bases announced earlier this year.

First Sea Lord, General Sir Gwyn Jenkins said it will allow the Navy to "tackle delays that hold us back" by "getting submarines through maintenance quicker and back where they belong: beneath the waves".

Harry Holt, Babcock's chief executive, said: "We are very proud at Babcock of the critical support that we provide to the Royal Navy, in particular our unwavering support to the continuous at sea deterrent – the UK's highest defence priority."

stories.body:
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali – the first Pakistani to reach orbit – greeted with Chinese ‘space handshake’ at Tiangong station

China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space station, starting what it says will be the globalisation of its space operations as the US-led International Space Station (ISS) enters its final years of operation.

Floating through a hatch to enter Tiangong, Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali grinned broadly as he was embraced by the onboard crew in what China’s space agency called the country’s first foreign “space handshake”.

Tiangong, completed in 2022, is the jewel in the crown of China’s space programme. The government has invested billions into its celestial ambitions in recent years to catch up with the US and Russia, two of the five partners involved in the ISS along with Europe, Japan and Canada. After 25 years of continuous occupation, the ISS is set to cease operations from 2030, according to Nasa.

On Wednesday China’s president, Xi Jinping, told his Pakistani counterpart that Beijing was “willing to work with all countries … to uphold the banner of the peaceful use of outer space”.

Ali was part of the crew of Shenzhou 24, the most recent iteration of the series of missions that rotate astronauts in the space station every six months. He is the first Pakistani to reach orbit.

Blaine Curcio, the managing director at Orbital Gateway Consulting, told the Guardian: “Sending another country’s astronaut to space is a major undertaking. Pakistan is putting a lot of trust into Beijing by having him fly into space on a Chinese-built rocket.

“There are also considerations related to security: Ali is getting detailed insights into China’s crewed space programme … It makes China better prepared to do it again, and also makes it clear to other countries that China is open to this type of collaboration.”

Space cooperation between China and Pakistan dates back to the early 1990s. China has launched Pakistani satellites, and a Pakistani-built rover ‌is due to fly on a Chinese lunar mission around 2028.

Shenzhou 24 blasted off from the Jiuquan launch centre in north-west China against a pink-tinged dawn sky on Wednesday and first docked with the space station three and a half hours later.

Ali, a 40-year-old Pakistan air force pilot and payload specialist, will conduct experiments including one cultivating microalgae as a potential food and another testing the effects of spaceflight on quinoa seeds. To prepare for the mission, he ​trained for seven months in Beijing, including taking intensive Chinese-language classes.

At a press conference the day before the launch, Ali recited a line from a classical Chinese poem. Commander Tang Hongbo told reporters that differences in language and culture had made learning to work together more challenging but that the effort had paid off.

Ali will not stay for the six-month term usually demanded of Tiangong astronauts. Instead, he will return to Earth with two of the Shenzhou 23 crew while its commander, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain to reach another milestone – the first full-year stay in space by a Chinese astronaut.

Beijing’s accelerated achievements in the skies have spooked its rivals. China is the third country to put humans in orbit and it has landed robotic rovers on Mars and the moon, where it hopes to send crewed missions within the next decade.

In racing to the moon before 2030, Beijing is competing with the US’s Artemis programme . The US has excluded China from the ISS since 2011, banning Nasa from collaborating with Beijing. In 2025, Nasa went further by blocking Chinese citizens from its facilities altogether.

US lawmakers have moved to try to extend the life of the ISS, citing China’s “permanent human presence in low Earth orbit” through Tiangong. Progress on turning that proposal into law has been slow. Nasa has said that after the ISS it will be “one of many customers in a robust commercial marketplace in low Earth orbit”.

The ISS was heralded as a symbol of post-cold war cooperation, but renewed cooperation with Russia seems “unlikely”, said Andrew Jones, a journalist specialising in China’s space programme.

While Tiangong is smaller than the ISS, China is understood to be preparing to double its size, “likely with the end of the ISS in mind”, Jones added. “These developments could allow China to expand its international engagement, and potentially space tourism. With the ISS nearing the end of its life and the future of western commercial space stations uncertain, China could for a time have the only permanently crewed outpost in low Earth orbit.”

China has long signalled its interest in developing Tiangong as an international hub. China Manned Space Agency documents published in coordination with the UN outline “resources for international cooperation” onboard the station. European and Chinese astronauts previously trained together with a view to a visit to Tiangong, but that cooperation ended for political and budgetary reasons, Jones said.

Curcio said he would expect countries such as Brazil and Egypt to seek out opportunities to send astronauts on Chinese missions. He added: “I think when the ISS is retired, if there is no western replacement (government or commercial), then yes, we may eventually see European or other ISS-involved countries – like Russia – send astronauts to Tiangong.”

stories.body:
Concerns over Beijing’s use of ‘red notices’ as Hong Kong prepares to host police organisation’s general assembly

China is misusing Interpol to target and silence dissidents, a leading British lawyer has claimed, as Hong Kong prepares to host the police organisation’s general assembly for the first time.

Ben Keith, a specialist in “red notices” - the Interpol system under which national authorities are requested to locate and detain suspects - said he was working on five cases involving China making questionable requests through Interpol.

He revealed that he had also contacted officials at the law enforcement organisation in July on behalf of a group of five high-profile UK-based Chinese dissidents to find out if Beijing had sought the issuance of red notices relating to them.

Interpol responded in October that they were looking into his request for information but there had been no substantive information shared, he added, raising concerns that there might be data relating to the individuals on the Interpol system.

He said: “If there’s no data, than they will tell me there’s no data. If there is data, then they have to get permission from Hong Kong to tell me. It has been sometime now. Given the profile of these individuals, I think they may have had some data on them. That’s the fear.”

Many Hong Kong democracy campaigners who fled to the UK in recent years have British national (overseas) status but this does not protect them from red notices outside the UK and potential extradition to China.

A red notice is a request to law enforcement worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender, or similar legal action. It is based on an arrest warrant or court order issued by the judicial authorities in the requesting country. Member countries apply their own laws in deciding whether to arrest a person.

Keith said: “The Russian playbook was to accuse political opponents or business opponents of some sort of really technical criminal offence of fraud, employment law breach, regulatory offence, that sort of thing, to disguise the real purpose of the request. The Chinese have taken that on.”

Hong Kong will host the 94th Interpol general assembly between 30 November and 3 December, attracting police chiefs from its 196 member countries to set global policing policy, approve budgets and activities, and pass binding resolutions.

Keith said that hosting the assembly offered an opportunity for China to “reputation wash”, arguing that Beijing ran a sophisticated public relations machine to hide the high proportion of red notice and extradition requests that were politically motivated.

The red notice system is used by China to target those sought under the state campaigns launched under President Xi Jinping to track down fugitives overseas and recover illicit funds, known as Operations Fox Hunt and Sky Net, it is claimed.

A new report , The Red Notice Trap, by Ben Keith and Rhys Davies of the legal firm IHR Advisors, draws on court judgments, Interpol records and Chinese-language official documents, to show how red notices fit into Beijing’s campaign to silence critics and bring them home for persecution.

It notes under a 2025 revision of the implementing regulations for the People’s Repubilc of China’s supervision law that red notice requests sit with extradition, judicial assistance, law enforcement cooperation, prosecution abroad, asset seizure and ‘ideological education’, as tools for the recovery of people.

Among the cases cited in the IHR Advisors report is that of Yidiresi Aishan – a Uyghur activist who is also known as Idris Hassan – who was arrested in July 2021, when arriving at Casablanca airport on a flight from Turkey, where he had been living.

He was detained on the basis of a red notice issued by Interpol at China’s request “for belonging to a terrorist organisation”. Within two weeks, Interpol suspended the notice as it breached its rules and it was later cancelled.

The Moroccan extradition proceedings carried on regardless and in December 2021 the country’s court of cassation approved Hasan’s surrender to China.

The UN committee against torture found that Hasan’s extradition would breach article 3 of the convention against torture and Morocco did not carry out the extradition But Hasan remained in detention until 12 February 2025 after spending nearly four years in prison on the basis of an Interpol red notice.

“His case shows the central weakness this report returns to: Interpol can correct its own data, but it cannot undo what national authorities have already set in motion”, the authors write.

Hasan, who now lives in Canada, said he no longer travelled and that his life had been thrown “upside down”.

“Four years of life have gone, just spent in prison, I could not be with my children,” he told the Guardian. “Everything has changed. I cannot describe this. But I trust Canada.”

Hasan added: “I don’t understand how this kind of the big organisation like Interpol how they took my name down without evidence, without nothing. Just put my name out.”

The Chinese embassy has been approached for comment.

An Interpol spokesperson said: “Interpol knows Red Notices are powerful tools for law enforcement cooperation and is fully aware of their potential impact on the individuals concerned, which is why Interpol has a number of systems in place to avoid misuse of our systems, and these have been significantly strengthened over the last few years.

“Interpol’s constitution affirms the Organisation’s neutrality. Under Article 3, Red Notice requests must not be of a predominantly political, military, religious or racial character.”

stories.body:
My friend and colleague David Collard, who has died aged 89, was an economist of unusual breadth: a theorist steeped in the history of ideas who never accepted that people act from self-interest alone.

Based at the University of Bath for nearly 25 years, he joined as professor of economics in 1978, becoming emeritus in 2002. He led the political economy group for 16 years (which later evolved into the economics department), headed the school of social sciences, and served as pro-vice-chancellor from 1989 to 1992. In those roles, he did much to raise the standing of the social sciences in a university built on science and engineering.

His most cited book, Altruism and Economy: A Study in Non-Selfish Economics (1978), challenged his discipline’s narrow model of rationality. He became a leading authority on key figures in the history of economics, such as Arthur Cecil Pigou, Francis Ysidro Edgeworth, Léon Walras and Sir John Hicks, and wrote on public finance and intergenerational justice. Beyond the university, he advised the government on the costs of tax compliance.

Born in Tiverton, Devon, David was the eldest of the three sons of Mildred (nee Ashton), a former glove factory worker, and Leslie Collard, a garage mechanic, who was away from the family in David’s early years, serving in north Africa and Italy during the second world war. At Tiverton grammar school David sat the civil service exam and was placed second in the country, but his headmaster persuaded him to try for Queens’ College, Cambridge.

National service came first at an RAF radar station in Germany, so David arrived at Queens’ in 1957 a little older than most. He was a scholar, ran cross-country for Cambridge University Hare & Hounds and took a first in economics. This brought invitations to interview at Manchester and Cardiff almost as soon as he graduated. He chose Cardiff, partly, he admitted, because they gave him a better lunch. There, on Guy Fawkes Night 1960, he met Stella Mackeson. They were engaged within five weeks and married in 1961.

After Cardiff, he joined Bristol University in 1964, moving to the University of Bath 14 years later. Colleagues there remember a man who wore his intellect lightly, was happy to shut down any committee he thought pointless, and preferred ideas and conversation to office.

In retirement in the hamlet of Pen-y-cae-mawr, near Usk in Monmouthshire, he and Stella kept bees, sheep and fruit trees, sang in the local choral society and acted in amateur dramatics, and he wrote a play, King Henry VII. He helped secure a bust of the Victorian naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace in Wallace’s birthplace of Usk, and his Christmas poems were a family fixture. He was a kind, generous spirit with brilliance, sharp insight, wit and resilience.

He is survived by Stella, their daughter, Jaki, grandchildren, Oliver, Celene and Bill, and great-grandchildren, Otis and Fern. David and Stella’s two sons, Peter and Paul, died in a boating accident in Devon in 1981.

Warning: contains graphic content some readers may find upsetting

“Parts of my body were still wet, and when I looked around as I lay on the ground, I realised this was from the blood of my family,” he says. “Saynab’s head was severed from the rest of her body. My children were unrecognisable. Their bodies were very burned and black, ripped to pieces.”

Still, as he lost consciousness again, he was sure who they were. “I knew they were my daughters, because the body parts strewn out in the cave were so small.”

The spread of cheap drones means warfare is increasingly conducted by invisible armies at the push of a button. Victims have no warning and no chance for justice

Death had come from the sky for Mohamed’s family: an execution carried out with no warning, no trial, no guilty verdict or chance for recourse.

He did not even know who had carried out the killing, or under which authority – several nations have drones patrolling the skies of Somalia looking for Islamic State militants, including the US, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Turkey and the Somali government. Any one of them could have pulled the trigger.

In Somalia, locals call these “ghost strikes” because the killer remains a phantom. With so many drones dropping bombs , and so many states (as well as non-state groups) operating their own drones, those being bombed may have little idea of who is killing them or precisely why.

Few countries publish data on where they carry out drone strikes, and even this is incomplete. Often, the only clues come from scattered fragments of bomb casings left behind, or what can be deduced from who is operating in the area or might have enemies there.

The phenomenon is a problem in countries far beyond Somalia. Ghost strikes reflect a fundamental shift in the way people conduct warfare. The machinery of war once required presence: soldiers on the ground or in the cockpit, tanks rolling through the streets, barracks and flags and bases. Only a small number of countries had the equipment – long-distance missiles and air forces – required to carry out a remote war, and those were relatively easy to monitor. Because most armies were physically present, there was also a stronger possibility of gathering evidence and holding them to account when it went terribly wrong: civilians massacred or war crimes committed.

Now, as cheap drones proliferate and become more accessible, thousands of civilians are being killed by remote control , at vast distances, sometimes by operators from countries with no boots on the ground at all. In Sudan’s brutal civil war, drones have rapidly overtaken ground troops as the leading cause of civilian death this year . Most often, no party takes responsibility for a strike. Last month, dozens of civilians were killed in strikes in Tigray, where Tigrayan, Ethiopian and Eritrean forces are all using drones – no one has claimed credit for the strikes or deaths.

On the Horn of Africa – which includes Somalia, Ethiopia and Sudan – the problem is playing out at a grand scale , with at least 11 nations or militant groups operating military drones in those three countries. But we are seeing the same thing in multiparty conflicts across the world, including Yemen, Iran, Myanmar and elsewhere.

According to new data from Drone Wars , more than 55 countries are now operating large, armed, predator-style drones, with seven other states due to acquire them soon. Chris Cole, director of Drone Wars, says this number is probably a significant undercount – the dataset doesn’t include the far cheaper one-way kamikaze models that detonate on impact, and there is nothing forcing countries or companies to announce when they have bought or sold drones, so many more could be acquiring them covertly.

Drones have also become stunningly cheap, in warfare terms. A US fighter jet costs between $80m (£66m) and $300m – amounts that once ensured air supremacy was the preserve of rich countries and centralised governments. But low-cost drones manufactured in Turkey and China are transforming the market, and creating a new set of drone superpowers. A Turkish-made medium altitude long endurance (Male) drone, which can conduct long-distance flights, is equipped with infrared cameras, stays airborne for more than 24 hours and carries more than about 130kg or 300lb of explosives, costs between $2m and $5m for each unit.

Since Turkey began introducing cheap predator-style military drones in the mid-2010s, followed by China in the 2020s, they have become new “drone superpowers” transforming the market and equipping dozens of new countries for air wars. Simpler drones, especially the kamikaze units, can now be bought for as little as $200, with hundreds of new drone startups entering the market, driven partly by the demand of the Russia-Ukraine war. The lower entry cost is shifting the balance of power in conflicts, inviting new players into air wars – even non-state actors including terrorist groups, militias and drug cartels are increasingly acquiring armed drones. It is also making it far harder to track who is killing who.

“The more they proliferate, the more state and non-state actors lay their hands on these cheap drones, the more it makes accountability then really, really difficult,” says Abdullahi Halakhe, an expert on security in the Horn of Africa and Great Lakes region. “This is now one of the biggest problems for civilian protection.”

For Mohamed to learn who had killed his family on 21 May, it would require identifying the bomb fragments, tracing them back to the country of manufacture and finding out who had bought them.

First, however, he had to survive.

Mobile reception is limited in the Golis mountains, and he knew the nearest mobile phone mast was 3 miles (5km) away. The only way to find help was to drag himself in that direction.

It was about noon when Abdullahi Omar, a resident in the nearby coastal town of Buruc, received a phone call saying something had happened in the mountains. The call came in from a nomad outside Baxaya who had come across Mohamed, terribly injured, at a river not far from the cave.

Immediately, Omar began organising a team of men to go out and investigate. “We prepared 36 men in town to go out to Baxaya,” he says.

double quotation mark Everyone who was picking up the body parts and wrapping up the remains had the sense that the same planes who massacred this family were now watching us.

The group of men trekked about 19 miles, leaving Buruc during afternoon prayers and walking through the night to reach the site of the strike the following morning. Among those who volunteered for the long hike through the mountains was Mohamed Hassan. “When we finally made it to Baxaya we came across the dead family and injured man,” he says. “There were no Daesh [Islamic State] fighters anywhere, only the bodies of women and children.”

The Golis mountains have been the centre of a global war against the Islamic State in Somalia, with the US carrying out hundreds of airstrikes in the region . The UAE has carried out strikes in the area, but does not publish any data on how many. And Turkey and Somalia’s governments are both also using Bayraktar drones for strikes in Somalia, but publish such minimal data that it is difficult to confirm exactly when or where.

Baxaya, where Mohamed and his family were hit, was supposedly designated a “safe zone” by the Puntland regional government – which was confirmed by Somalia’s deputy ambassador to Tanzania, Ashkir Nuur, who represents the constituency.

“The Puntland authorities have not apologised nor compensated the sole survivor. It happened under their jurisdiction but the sole survivor is yet to receive answers,” Nuur says.

Local people say there were no Islamic State fighters nearby, and Male drone systems are equipped with sensitive, infrared camera systems for monitoring targets that should make it easy to distinguish a fighting force from a family with young children and 250 goats. Who, then, carried out the strike?

The men gathered up the pieces of Mohamed’s children, wrapping them in cloth for burial. As they worked, they heard the insect moan of drones above.

“While collecting the body parts of the family members, we could hear loud engines of planes – we couldn’t see them but could hear,” Hassan says. “Everyone who was picking up the body parts and wrapping up the remains had the sense that the same planes who massacred this family were now watching us.”

The men worked as quickly as they could. They took a series of photos and videos to document the strike’s aftermath, showing the bodies of Seynab, Fadumo, Aman and Anab, and the strewn bodies of dead goats. Photographs and video of the strike site taken by these first responders and reviewed by the Guardian confirm Mohamed’s description of events, including the catastrophic blast injuries to his wife, her unborn child, their three daughters, and the subsequent explosion that killed hundreds of his goats. The Guardian is not publishing these images due to their graphic nature.

In a video from the scene, one man stands before the four wrapped bodies, after they have been prepared for burial, and says: “The missile massacred the people right here, and as you have been told, these are their bodies. We want the world to watch this and know.”

Among the drying blood and debris, the men found something else: the shattered pieces of two missile casings, lying in the dirt. With no country claiming responsibility for the strike on the family, these dusty chunks of metal would provide the only evidence trail between the family who died, their killers and the booming, multibillion-dollar industry that provided the equipment.

Independent munitions experts Trevor Ball and NR Jenzen-Jones, of Armament Research services, have analysed the images of bomb fragments left at the scene for the Guardian and concluded that they are from a MAM-series munition, manufactured by the Turkish state-owned defence manufacturer Roketsan.

Jenzen-Jones says the “bomb remnants pictured probably evidence a strike by an unmanned aerial vehicle [UAV], mostly likely a Bayraktar TB2”.

The drone is named for its creator – Selçuk Bayraktar, one of the stars of Turkey’s drone industry. His company, Baykar, has had a meteoric rise since it brought the first Bayraktar drone on to the global market in 2014, and works closely with state-owned defence companies, arming its drones with Rokestan munitions. In 2016, Bayraktar married Sümeyye Erdoğan, the daughter of the president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, in a lavish wedding ceremony, drawing Baykar into even closer connection with its government.

Turkey is a relatively recent entrant to the drone market, but it has rapidly dominated sales to new states buying large, predator-style drones – particularly across African and Arab countries. On the back of its drone manufacturers, the country’s entire defence export market has boomed, reaching more than £7.5bn last year , up more than 500% from a decade earlier . The country now claims to control 65% of the global drone market , and Baykar has become one of the world’s biggest military drone companies. This year, the country’s military exports are tracking toward a new record high.

At the same time, Turkey has developed a reputation for relatively lax “no questions asked” export rules. A large portion of the governments that Turkey has sold drones to in the past five years are classed as fully authoritarian regimes (including Mali, Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan, Rwanda, Turkmenistan, Qatar, Uzbekistan, Chad, Togo, Niger, Tunisia, Djibouti, Burkina Faso, Kuwait, Libya, Somalia) and/or already embroiled in civil war or armed internal conflict (including but not limited to Sudan, Ethiopia, Nigeria, Somalia) . Numerous states on Turkey’s customer list have subsequently been accused of mass killings of civilians using their equipment. For Ankara, however, the explosion of the drone market has been a geopolitical success – with Turkey leveraging drone sales to massively grow its overseas political and military influence.

A Turkish diplomatic representative said: “Turkish UAV exports to Sudan or Somalia, like those to other countries, are subject to guarantees that they will be used in full compliance with international law. There is no verified information indicating that Turkish-manufactured UAVs have been used in violation of the relevant international norms and regulations by the Sudanese Army or in Somalia.”

Even tracing the missile that killed Mohamed’s family to its source, however, does not tell us who was responsible for pulling the trigger. The UAE, Turkey and the Somali government all fly Bayraktar drones in Somali skies. The US has also carried out hundreds of strikes in the region, but using its own drones.

The Turkish, Somali and UAE governments did not respond to requests for comment on who dropped the bomb on Mohamed and his family. Here, the trail runs cold. Seynab, Aman, Anab and Fadumo’s killers remain ghosts.

Hours after they arrived, the men began the long trek back through the mountains toward the coast. Hassan was one of those who carried Mohamed, hauling his body over the difficult, rocky terrain of the mountains for more than 24 hours.

The whole way, the sound of planes followed them.

“It would go away, then once again the noise would return, so we knew our every step was being watched,” Hassan says. “We were scared because we knew what the planes did to Mohamed and his family … They were innocent people, who did nothing wrong and were massacred by these same planes now hovering above us.” From Buruc, the company sent Mohamed on a raft to Bosaso, the nearest equipped hospital, for treatment.

Before Mohamed had even arrived at the hospital, Abdulkadir Koudah, a family member, had heard the news and contacted local security services to inform them that a man who was the sole survivor of an airstrike was on his way. In the months since, “they haven’t helped us or given us any answers on who bombed the family”, he says.

Mohamed is slowly recovering, although the wounds are still visible on his body. Still, he says: “The burns on my body are nothing compared to what my daughters went through.

“They were excited about having another sibling and so was their mother, but everything changed in the blink of an eye and I don’t know who to blame.”

stories.body:
After the CEO was reinstated after Trump’s pressure campaign, it is abundantly clear: there are different rules for rich people

T here are different rules for rich people. If you or I acted the way that Jensen Huang has been accused of acting – allegedly berating and mistreating employees, sleeping with subordinates, and seeming to carry on a staggering number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman identified by US intelligence as a likely Chinese spy who helped smuggle the company’s product to China – we probably would find ourselves out of work and out of favor for quite some time.

But this is not so for Huang, the tech founder and close ally to Donald Trump who was recently ousted from Nvidia, the chip manufacturer he founded. On Monday, after a pressure campaign from Donald Trump, JD Vance and other members of the Trump administration , Huang was reinstated as CEO by the Nvidia board.

His alleged actions had risked national security; his fall from power lasted less than two weeks.

According to early reporting, Trump decided late last week to intervene in Huang’s case, thinking that his restoration as Nvidia’s chief could help rally a sluggish stock market. In an economy that has become increasingly dependent on the success of AI companies, Nvidia , which makes the chips that enable the technology, has come to be seen as something of a load-bearing firm, propping up an AI sector which is increasingly understood to be in an overvaluation bubble that will inevitably pop.

“The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company but the American Economy,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. The reinstatement was reportedly orchestrated by Vance, the vice-president and presumptive 2028 Republican nominee, who drew on his own deep ties to friends, allies and benefactors in Silicon Valley to convey the administration’s strong desire for Huang to return.

It marks a remarkable intervention of the executive branch into the personnel decisions of a private firm.

In public statements, Huang’s allies and boosters have repeatedly emphasized the restored CEO as personally essential to the company, downplaying the national security and chip-smuggling concerns in favor of a portrait of a singular mind.

Huang, they say, is unique and irreplaceable, essential to the functioning of Nvidia and hence of the economy; because of this supposed personal specialness, we’re told, it makes sense if he got to spill secrets to China over pillow talk at the expense of your retirement fund.

But it is striking that this deep belief in the irreplaceable brilliance of one AI CEO is so profoundly at odds with the ethos of the AI industry, which promises to automate away all human judgment and experience and make human beings in general – let along any one human being in particular – profoundly replaceable, if not completely superfluous.

Maybe this, too, is another way that the rules are different for the rich: the tech executives never meant to say that they themselves would become disposable and interchangeable. That fate was reserved for the lowly, like you and me.

It is just this sort of shocking arrogance and display of elite impunity among the tech sector that has disgusted Americans and shocked their consciences; the deep and emphatic rejection of datacenters that was expressed by voters in the recent midterm elections should be understood, I think, as a proxy for a bigger discontent with the recklessness and greed of the tech oligarchs who impose their whims on the country with life-altering consequences.

It is not clear, either, why the Trump administration, which claims that national security and the US economy rely on the returns of AI companies, would want one of the most important of those companies to be helmed by a man who may have been compromised by China, the nation’s primary adversary and main economic competitor.

The flagrancy of the seeming corruption and incompetence at play, and the evident rage of the American people at both, will hopefully spur Democrats to launch serious and probing investigations into Nvidia, Huang and their ties to the Trump administration when the party takes control of both houses of Congress in January.

In the meantime, Trump himself has indicated that there’s one reason why he has taken a particular interest in Huang’s case: sex. In a statement to the Times, Trump said that he thought Huang had been treated unfairly because of the sexual nature of his scandal, or what the president called “The Peyton Place part” – an evident reference, the Times helpfully explained to its less senior readers, to a 1960s soap opera that featured many sex scandals.

“Without that, it would have been a lot easier,” Trump said, “because that got the attention. You know, sex was involved, and sex sells better than stocks.” Call it a kind of sex-pest solidarity. The president, a habitual adulterer who has been accused of sexual misconduct by more than two dozen women and who paid an adult film star to keep quiet about their alleged affair (all of which he denies), seems to see something of himself in the prolifically and allegedly perhaps treasonably adulterous Jensen Huang. Elite impunity may have extra appeal when it can double as male impunity, too.

As if to emphasize the point, Trump took to Truth Social to share an AI-generated image of Jensen Huang, in a pose mimicking a famous photograph of Trump himself rising up in the moments after an assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, in the summer of 2024. In the original photo, Trump held up a fist in triumph, showing that he had survived the gunman’s shots. In the new version that the president posted on Monday morning, Huang held up a red bra.

Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist
